#5611. If You Thought The Cybertruck Was Ugly, Get A Load Of This EV On Rails

The ill-fated Tesla Cybertruck has been roundly excoriated for its dumpster-adjacent profile, but it looks pretty good compared to the EVs rolling out of the shop at the Missouri-based startup Intramotev. However, looks are not everything. Intramotev is on a mission to chase diesel fuel off the nation’s nation’s rail freight system, and its “TugVolt” autonomous electrified freight cars get the job done, aesthetically pleasing or not.

Intramotev surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar back in 2023 with two retrofit products. One is the ReVolt, a battery pack that can be slotted onto existing railcars hauled behind a locomotive, with the aim of saving diesel fuel. The other, more interesting retrofit is the TugVolt, an autonomous, electrified system that enables railcars to go about the business of hauling freight on their own, without a locomotive.

While the battery packs in each TugVolt have a limited range, that’s more than enough to accomplish a good day’s work including “first mile” loading duties. Once loaded up, they can hitch a ride on locomotives for long-distance travel, then split off to unload.

In addition, a freight yard that hosts a full complement of autonomous railcar EVs would require little, if any, participation from diesel-powered switcher locomotives. In addition to hauling its own freight, each TugVolt can also operate as a switcher, ferrying conventional railcars into position behind a locomotive.

The technology also has significant implications for decarbonizing highway freight as well. The closer an electric railcar can get to its destination, the less need there is for a diesel-fueled truck to pick up the slack. In particular, Intramotev is focusing on captive or short line routes, many of which have seen their rail traffic shrink in the face of competition from the trucking industry.

Intramotev has been rather busy over the past three years. In one particularly interesting development, in June Intramotev lent a TugVolt to a US Army Reserve Training exercise at the Camp Shelby Joint Forces Training Center in Mississippi, billed as the largest training exercise in the history of the Army Reserve.

“Soldiers, according to Intramotev, trained on and operated the TugVolt system under company supervision throughout the exercise and quickly became proficient with the technology, a detail that matters because military rail operations have traditionally required specialized rail crews, a category of personnel the Army has struggled to maintain at sufficient strength given how infrequently large-scale rail movements occur outside major deployment exercises,” reports the independent news and analysis organization Defence Blog.

As noted by Defence Blog, the exercise went off script when railcars loaded with military supplies arrived at the site. However, with their training freshly in hand, the participants were able to deploy the TugVolt to organize the incoming railcars for unloading.

It’s no surprise to find Intramotev in Texas, too, considering the state’s reputation as a hot EV market. On November 3, the company expanded its ongoing relationship with Watco, a holding company specializing in short line railways.

The new arrangement calls for TugVolt to pull zero emission switcher duty at a to-be-named industrial facility in Seadrift, Texas. As noted by Railway Age, the Texas assignment adds to Intramotev’s EV footprint in the US, which also includes Michigan as well as the Army demonstration in Missouri, and a forthcoming agreement in Kentucky.

Railway Age further notes that in April, Intramotev lent itself to electrification efforts in Austria. That’s a particularly significant development because the client is ÖBB, the national railway of Austria, making it the first deployment of TugVolt technology under regulation, in addition to Intramotev’s first overseas client.

The agreement is also significant considering ÖBB’s sprawling footprint in Europe, consisting of more than 1,000 freight trains ranging across 18 countries every day.

Even more significant, at least from a policy perspective, is a $16.3 million grant from the Federal Railroad Administration branch of the US Department of Transportation. US taxpayers will shoulder the bulk of the cost-sharing arrangement, which is designed to model best practices for introducing EVs into the nation’s railway system. The project is hosted by the Columbia Terminal Railroad, a city-owned, 21.4 mile line that links two cities in Missouri, Columbia and Centralia.

“The project will deploy autonomous railcars on the line to produce the first documented safety record for autonomous railcar operation and create a workforce training curriculum,” FRA emphasizes.

“The proposed project was selected for Project Development, Final Design, and Construction and involves research and workforce development activities to conduct a phased autonomous rail technology and short-line infrastructure modernization program,” FRA elaborates, further noting that the EV project “aligns with the selection criteria by improving system and service performance,” with the ultimate goal of enabling freight to run more frequently and, ultimately, autonomously.

Of note, the grant of up to $16 million or so is part of a $2.3 billion railway CRISI modernization package, with CRISI being short for Infrastructure and Safety Improvements. Among other purposes, CSRISI “provides a Federal funding opportunity to “mitigate congestion at both intercity passenger rail and freight rail chokepoints to support more efficient travel and goods movement.”

Citing Intramotev official Don Soffer, the local news organization News Tribune notes that “more than 600 short lines in the U.S. have declined in use in recent decades due to their relative inefficiency.”

“Cross-country hauling is more profitable for companies, whereas short lines require very large hauls to justify the quick trip. The Columbia Terminal Railroad (COLT) does not operate on a set schedule, instead hauling whenever enough goods are collected,” the News Tribune continues.

Given that context, if the CSRISI grant is not a decarbonization program for short line railways and associated highway traffic, I’ll eat my hat. It’s also worth noting that practically the entire locomotive fleet of the US runs on a diesel-electric platform, meaning electric motors powered by an on-board generator. While fossil energy is still in play, the diesel-electric configuration is more energy efficient than sending fleets of diesel trucks onto the nation’s highways.

The nation’s trucking industry has also been wrestling with an ongoing driver shortage, providing further motivation to move more freight onto rails, EVs or not.

Stay tuned for updates on that Missouri project. FRA announced its selection for Project Development, Final Design, and Construction in October, so there are still steps to take before the TugVolt begins running.

Meanwhile, circling back around to that Army demo in June, more likely than not the hookup with the US DoD will not be a one-off. The Army has been notoriously slow to adopt EVs, and last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy did not help. Still, the Army has been sending out EV signals through its use of new “anti-idling” kits for ground vehicles, alongside a new contract with the US branch of the firm Rheinmetall for a fleet of crewless hybrid cargo haulers. Again, looks are not everything…

#5610. Stellanis Confirms Nearly All Its Racing Programs Are Dead

Peugeot might have major racing victories in three different centuries, but that heritage wasn't enough to save its Le Mans Hypercar program. Stellantis announced on Monday that it's pulling the plug on all its factory motorsports programs, confirming last week's reports. The automotive giant won't fully shutter the motorsport division, hoping to still generate revenue from customer racing. The only projects to avoid the axe were its North American subsidiary's revived NASCAR efforts under the Dodge and Ram brands.

Stellantis stated it intends to "refocus its motorsport activities and resources on customer racing and high-performance vehicle development." Amid the company's dire financial situation, CEO Antonio Filosa set a goal early this year of $6.6 billion in cost savings by 2028. The decision was sudden for the programs. Peugeot planned to compete with an updated 9X8 in next year's FIA World Endurance Championship and had already begun testing the new prototype. With Alpine's previously announced departure, this means there will be no French manufacturer in the top class of the 2027 24 Hours of Le Mans.

There were two silver linings to Stellantis' decision. First, the company will be continuing its customer racing programs. Second, the company's two Formula E teams will be allowed to contest the upcoming season. Citroën and Opel collaborated in developing new cars for the debut Gen4 campaign. These 800-horsepower machines will get a single season in the sun (or rain) before getting sent to the scrap heap. It's a similar situation to what happened to Lancia's WRC2 program, with the Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale running its maiden season this year before Stellantis pulled the plug.

As much as some auto executives champion the "win on Sunday, sell on Monday" mentality, the exposure of being in a motorsport series only truly exists if you're competing in the front half of the field. Using Formula 1 as an example, Aston Martin and Cadillac might as well not exist to TV cameras unless their cars crash or get lapped by the leaders. Saving the Peugeot 9X8 program would be a hard sell for anyone because LMH went five years without winning a WEC race or finishing a Le Mans podium.

#5609. Texas Drops Lawsuits Accusing Docs of Illegally Providing Transgender Care to Minors

— State was the first to bring cases against doctors

Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is ending efforts to punish two doctors who were among the first in the U.S. to face accusations of violating bans on providing care to transgender youth, dropping the cases as the Republican prepares to leave office following a failed Senate run.

The lawsuits against the doctors, which were filed in 2024, were among a spate of high-profile cases that helped Paxton burnish his image as a conservative fighter but are now winding down as Democrats prepare to retake power in Texas for the first time in decades.

The state's lawsuits against May Lau, MD, MPH, and M. Brett Cooper, MD, were dismissed Friday, according to attorneys for the doctors. They were among three doctors who Paxton called "scofflaws" and "radical gender activists" in lawsuits that threatened to impose steep fines and revoke their medical licenses.

"Dr. Lau did nothing wrong, but she was a convenient scapegoat for the Attorney General's Office, which issued press release after press release about its case -- a case that has now collapsed," Nicole LeBoeuf, an attorney for Lau, said in a statement.

LeBoeuf said the timing of the dismissal after Paxton's loss "validates that this case against Dr. Lau was political from beginning to end." Lau moved her medical practice from Dallas to Oregon during the lawsuit.

In January, Democrat Nathan Johnson will become Texas' next attorney general.

Paxton's office did not immediately return a request for comment Monday.

Texas Was the First State to Bring Cases Against Doctors

Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump, dropped another lawsuit last year against a third doctor, Hector Granados, MD, and his office later said the El Paso pediatric endocrinologist did not break the law.

Texas' ban on gender-affirming care for transgender youths took effect in 2023. And while other states have prohibitions on gender-affirming care for transgender youth, Texas was the first to bring cases against doctors, filing lawsuits against the three providers.

Trump launched a broad charge against transgender rights in his second term, moving to reverse years of legal and policy gains for transgender Americans. Even in states where the care is allowed under state law, major hospitals and hospital systems have said they were stopping or restricting the care.

Cooper, a Dallas physician, "has always maintained that he acted lawfully and in the best interests of his patients," his attorneys, Simona Agnolucci and Anika Holland, said in a statement.

Other lawsuits Paxton's office has dropped since his Senate loss include those against out-of-state doctors for sending abortion pills to Texas.

Paxton and Republicans Leaned Into Transgender Attacks During Midterms

In the final phase of this year's midterm elections, Republicans spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats, according to tallies provided to the Associated Press by data firm AdImpact. Texas' Senate contest between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico consumed the largest share of that spending, drawing an estimated $58 million for more than 50,000 airings before the election, according to AdImpact.

The GOP focus on transgender issues stood in stark contrast with what voters told pollsters they cared most about in the midterm season, which included the state of the economy.

#5608. Robotics component maker coprod raises $6M to take on robotics ‘integration hell’

Robotics component maker coprod Inc. announced today that it has raised $6 million in new funding to reduce the time and costs associated with building new robotic platforms.

The funding is intended to enable the company to bring its first line of components to market. Founded in 2024, coprod offers an ecosystem of compatible hardware components for robotics and physical artificial intelligence applications.

It works alongside a software application programming interface and a front-end configuration tool to interconnect the components and standardize the communication between them, while preserving the real-time performance required for safe and reliable hardware.

At the core of coprod’s offering is the co:system, which combines the company’s modules on a single real-time EtherCAT control plane with one API in C++ and Python. The product family includes co:power, co:battery, co:sensor and co:motion, with each module able to be used as part of a complete system or integrated on its own.

Coprod is tackling the issue wherein most component suppliers support many protocols in the hope of catering to any integrator, which means their parts rarely work together out of the box. The result, according to coprod, is that building a system from mix-and-match components puts a heavy burden on the integrator. It requires two to three years of custom electronics and software work common before a system is reliable, in a phase known in the industry as “integration hell.”

The company claims that with its stack, the same work requires only a small team of roboticists, $5,000 to $25,000 per design iteration and a few months of time.

“We believe that a robot with purpose-built hardware designed for a specific task will do that task faster, cheaper and more reliably than any general purpose robot ever could, regardless of which model runs on it,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Loïc Delineau.

Coming into its new funding round, coprod’s components are already powering multiple robots in Switzerland, including the ETH Robotics Club’s XALUN, the first student-built Swiss humanoid robot, which took its first steps in Zurich in recent weeks. The company is also establishing partnerships with robotics integrators and well-known labs to validate its first hardware prototypes before launching them on the market early next year.

The funding is also intended to support a new hardware prototyping facility in Lausanne. Equipped with CNC lathes, mills, lasers and electronic assembly and testing equipment, the workshop is expected to cut the company’s development cycles from two weeks to 24 hours. Testing at the site will be used to produce datasheets and digital twin models for each component, an effort aimed at narrowing the gap between simulated and real-world performance that arises in robotics development.

By the end of 2027, coprod plans to have its entire component line on the market, qualified and certified. Large-scale production is planned for both Shenzhen and Texas, with the company’s headquarters and research and development remaining in Switzerland.

Component supply has also emerged as a constraint for robot makers, particularly in humanoids. A McKinsey & Co. analysis published in April found that supply chain bottlenecks for humanoids are most likely to emerge around actuators and sensing and perception systems, the type of hardware coprod is developing.

Delineau formed coprod with Chief Technology Officer Vincent Nguyen and Chief Scientist Matthias Schuller (pictured), all graduates of the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne. The three started out by building a bipedal robot demonstrator in a parent’s garage in the Swiss Alps to show what compatible components could do.

Founderful AG and Prototype Capital led the pre-seed round, with General Catalyst Group Management, Pace Ventures, Tiny Supercomputer Investment Company, Kima Ventures, SDAC, Unruly Capital and Venture Kick also participating. Angel investors in the round include Hugging Face Inc. co-founder Thomas Wolf, the Dassault family and Florent Perrichon. Venture Kick awarded coprod CHF 40,000 ($47,600) earlier this year.

Andreas Klinger, founder of Prototype, said coprod is fixing “the biggest problem in hardware.” It argues that robotics founders need a single standard for basic components and middleware so they can focus on the parts of their products that create value for customers.

#5607. 90 New Vehicle Models Were Just Introduced in Colombia’s Largest Automotive Exhibition. 55 Were Electric.

The last two weeks, the future was on display in Bogota’s Automobile Hall.

This Hall is Colombia’s largest and most important Automotive Exhibition, and since 2023 (17th edition, held after a hiatus of 5 years), it has heralded the unstoppable tide of EVs progressively taking over the national market. Back then, despite EVs making up less than 3% of the market, EVs were already present and relevant in the Automobile Hall, with the Changan Lumin being a particularly bright star.

EVs have been gaining ground since, with more of them arriving every year, and in the latest iteration of the Automobile Hall, we’ve reached a point of no return: EVs make up a majority of the newly announced models arriving in the country. Or to be specific: out of 90 arrivals, EVs account for 55!

32 brands brought new electric or plug-in hybrid cars to showcase in Bogota’s Automobile Hall. Even though most of them (unsurprisingly) are from China, we still find presences from 7 European and 2 Japanese brands here — all will be listed at the end of this article with their respective models.

Most of these models arrive at very competitive pricing, many times undercutting their direct gasoline and diesel competition, and with ever-improving specs — by reasonable standards, most of these cars should be able to make at least 350 km on Colombian roads, making them quite appealing options even for people who travel regularly.

Colombia’s EV market share has been growing in 2026, reaching 20% — or almost — every month since March. But with this EV avalanche (or EV-lanche), I think it’s inevitable that we will see that number go up in the months to come — though how fast exactly, I leave to you to debate.

And no, you were not the only ones to notice that there are exactly zero (0) arrivals from US brands. Tesla was of course present, but with nothing new (though they did present the Cybercab at a later date than I attended), other than Tesla, US brands are either too small or too focused on gas-guzzlers to bother even trying to compete.

Note: all prices mentioned here include taxes, but registration and insurance may not be included.

I will start with the non-Chinese EVs, because, well, they’re fewer.

The most important model here, by far, is the Renault 4 e-Tech. People outside this country probably don’t know that the Renault 4 was built here for 22 years, becoming the most affordable car for decades and a symbol of the Colombian middle class. Nicknamed the “Colombian Car” and the “Loyal Friend,” the Renault 4 has a place in the hearth of most Colombians, and, as such, the R4 e-Tech was one of the most visited cars in the entire exhibition.

Because of this, it’s certain that the car will have some buyers. But at 100 million COP (€26,000, $28,500), it’s a hard sell, particularly when the hatchback segment has stabilized somewhere around $20,000 for Chinese models. Nostalgia has a price for sure, but not that many people will be willing to pay $8,500 for it.

The BMW iX3 was also present in the hall, and I must admit it’s a very compelling and impressive car, but at 300 million COP ($85,400), there are not a lot of buyers that will be interested.

From the European side, other than Renault and BMW, we have the Cupra Terramar and the Mini Cooper SE Paul Smith Edition, both around 160 million COP (€41,700, $45,500). So, quite expensive for their segments, even though I find the Terramar a very beautiful car. The Porsche Cayenne is of course expensive beyond anything seen prior, and the Volvo EX60 has not announced pricing yet. As for Stellantis, it’s betting on its two vans, somewhat expensive but still viable, and it has the Opel Crossland EV, which has been on the market for a while but is now discounted to 90 million COP (€23,400, $25,600), meaning it’s one of the most competitive non-Chinese EVs available.

Regarding the Japanese, the Toyota BZ4X (already present) and the RAV4 PHEV (just arriving) are of course important players, but at 220 million and 270 million COP respectively ($62,600 and $76,800), they won’t sell more than a trickle of units. The Nissan Frontier Pro has the same price as the BZ4X, and, to be fair, I didn’t even notice it was available until I left the Hall.

Paradoxically, the most competitive non-Chinese EVs all come from a brand with zero arrivals: Kia. With its EV2 starting at 90 million COP and its EV3 at 120 million COP ($23,400 and $34,100), Kia has the closest prices to any Chinese competitor and can at least rely on the brand’s popularity to keep some of the market.

With that out of the way, let’s look at the Chinese arrivals, or at least some of them, as there are too many to mention.

You can see the full list of models at the end of the article. Here I will focus on those I think will make the most impact in the market.

First, one of my favorite EVs: the all-mighty Chery ICaur V23. In a previous article I mentioned how surprising its low range was … but I must admit I judged it rashly. I mean, that thing is huge. I really expected it to be much smaller, and thus I understand why it can barely edge a 360 km range (WLTP) despite a sizeable 81 kWh battery. When you’re built like a small tank, you can expect to get the range of a small tank, no surprises here.

But the great selling point for this car is its price: 85 million COP for the 4×2 version and 105 million COP for the 4×4 version ($24,100 and $29,900). We’re talking a fully off-road capable SUV for the same or less than a Renault 4 or a Corolla. Truly impressive, and an example of EV innovation in segments that many other OEMs have not dared enter, assuming they are lost to the ICEV competition.

BYD also surprised by bringing a new Sealion RWD, armed with a 70 kWh battery and aimed directly against the Model Y. At 115 million COP ($32,700), this car is $1,500 cheaper than the Model Y RWD while having a larger battery and better range. It seems the Chinese giant wants to start getting back some market share a year after the US brand took the market by storm. Better late than never I guess.

BYD is also bringing the EREV Leopard 7 under its own brand (BYD Ti7), but at 225 million COP ($64,000), it will certainly not be a best seller, even though it will probably give the likes of Toyota and Land Rover a run for their money.

Now, my dear readers, I hope you will forgive me here, but even though I actually went to the Hall to take a look to the XPeng Mona L03 specifically, it seems I got distracted by the robot and the drone-licopter, and thus this is the picture you’re getting … because I forgot to take one of the L03. Regardless, the XPeng L03 is also pointing directly at Tesla, arriving at 115 million COP ($32,700), the same price of the entry-level Model 3, except the L03 provides full self-driving capabilities for this price, to the extent that XPeng can provide that of course. This car (available in BEV and PHEV versions) and the BYD Sealion are poised to bring a significant challenge not only to Tesla, but to the entire ICEV ecosystem, which is having evermore competition in its bread-and-butter segments by the month.

There are currently 6 subcompact entry-level SUVs fighting in the 80-to-95 million COP segment: the Chery Omoda E5, the MG S5, the Dongfeng Vigo, the Faw Bestune Joy, the Changan Nevo Q05, and the Ora 5.

I chose the Ora 5 to represent the segment because it offers the largest battery (58kWh, vs 50kWh for all the others) and, as of the Automobile Hall, the lowest price for the entry-level version, at only 73 million COP (USD $20.800). This is a true bargain, making it the cheapest available SUV of any powertrain by quite some distance, and a very compelling option for budget-oriented buyers. It remains to be seen if this price will remain after the Hall.

Going by specs alone, I believe the JMEV GSX to be the best value-for-money vehicle currently available in the Colombian market. This SUV boasts an impressive 70 kWh battery with 500 km WLTP range for a mere 90 million COP ($25,600). The only thing against it is that JMEV (JMC) is quite a small brand and has not gained traction in this market, or in any other that I know of.

In Colombia, this minicar has taken the place that belonged to the Wuling Hongguang in China, and more recently belongs to the Chery QQ Ice Cream — that of a (barely) highway-capable minicar that may seat four, or two plus your groceries, but that will fit in any spot and can be parked wherever you may find a square meter available. Available with a brand new 18.1 kWh battery, the Faw Xiaoma 2.0 remains the most affordable “true” car in Colombia at 40 million COP ($11,400).

It’s worth noting that Faw has failed to gain traction in the Colombian market, and it clearly wanted to change that in this Hall, as it brought an entire armada, with its N09 Sedan available for 100 million COP ($28,300) as its flagship car.

Aside from minicars (like the Xiaoma above), the Dongfeng Box deserves a mention for being the cheapest car in the hatchback segment at 65 million COP ($18,500). With its 42 kWh battery, it can reasonably travel long distance with the current infrastructure. I’ve ridden in both this car and the Geely EX2, and, frankly, the EX2 has a higher quality feel, but this one is slightly cheaper, and no doubt this will bring some buyers.

At a price of only 75 million COP ($21,350), the Foton e-Wonder mini-truck provides full price parity with diesel versions and opens the possibility of electrification for the owners of smaller companies. At 1-ton carrying capacity, it’s a very compelling vehicle, even if its 40 kWh battery remains limited for long-distance operations.

Of course, this list would not be complete without the most affordable “real” car here (so, not minicars included, sorry Xiaoma!). The Jac E10X is a city-car available for 60 million COP ($17,000), and even though it looks good and has decent quality, it has never sold well because JAC is not a very popular brand, and because its 30 kWh battery lacks capacity for making even medium-distance trips without having at least some range anxiety.

Well, this is it. My apologies for the fans of Arcfox and Leapmotor — both are very important brands arriving in the country, but Arcfox lacks recognition and prices are a bit over the competition (they are a luxury brand, but that may not convince people who don’t already know them) and Leapmotor only brought EREVs, and as you may have seen, I focused on BEVs in the very long Chinese list.

My conclusions are probably quite predictable. China is leading and by quite an advantage, the Koreans are not too far behind, the Europeans are trying to make a comeback, the Japanese are making a symbolic (but useless) stand, and the Americans — other than Tesla — didn’t even bother to show up.

It’s hard to believe only three years have passed since Bogota’s Automobile Hall of 2023, when the Changan Lumin was the star and when we were celebrating going over 2% market share. Back then, EVs were still expensive, charging infrastructure was much more limited, and the mainstream was firmly on the pure-combustion side, with hybrids making some inroads.

Now, after the EV-lanche we’re seeing, it seems that EVs are now fully in the mainstream, with lower prices and better specs than ever before. EV sales will keep growing fast, and I expect the market to tilt even more to the side of zero-emissions transportation in the coming months. 30% BEV market share is now well within sight.

For those of you who want to look at the full list of arrivals, here it is below. BEVs are in bold, PHEVs and EREVs are in regular.

Arcfox T5, T1, S5; Avatr 11, 7; BAIC X55; BYD Sealion RWD, Ti7 (Leopard 7), Atto 8; Deepal S09; Denza Z9 GT, B5; Dongfeng 7, 8; Farizon V7E, F3E; Faw Xiaoma 2.0, Joyee N09, Joyee S08; Foton E-Tunland; GAC Aion UT 2027, S7; Geely Monjaro EM-I, Starray EM-R; GWM Tank 700, ICaur V23, V27; IM IM6; Jetour G700, T2; JMEV GSX; Leapmotor B10, C10; Lynk & Co 2, 1, 8, 900; MHero II; Rox Motor 1; Xpeng L03, L03; Zeekr 007GT, 001FR, 9X.

BMW iX3, iX5, i7; Cupra Terramar; Mini Cooper SE Paul Smith; Peugeot E-Partner, Peugeot E-Expert; Porsche Cayenne; Renault R4 E-Tech; Volvo EX60.

#5606. Maybe Just Stay Off The Roads This Thanksgiving, Folks

The weeks surrounding the Thanksgiving holiday are some of the busiest travel days of the year in the United States. This year, AAA projects that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home between Tuesday November 24 and Monday, November 30, and it projects that 72.8 million of those Americans will be making that drive by car. That's actually a slight drop from last year's result of 73.1 million travelers, but AAA says travelers in major metropolitan areas could still expect to see more than double the normal traffic congestion. We think that may even be a conservative estimate, given that weather forecasts across the country tell a stormy story.

A coastal flood advisory has been issued for the Pacific Northwest and parts of Northern California, and there's currently a nor'easter storm that looks like it will bring heavy rains, winds, and coastal flooding to the entire East Coast over the course of Wednesday and Thursday. The mayor of San Francisco even posted a video to social media urging people to avoid unnecessary travel, saying, "If you don't need to, please don't travel into the city. We always want visitors, but these are special circumstances." We got all your wet weather driving tips to help folks prepare for the Super El Niño a few months ago, so feel free to revisit that if you can't avoid driving in stormy conditions.

The National Weather Service determined that the nor'easter storm strengthening off the southeastern coast could undergo rapid cyclogenesis and become a bomb cyclone by Thanksgiving day. It's also expected to bring powerful winds with gusts of over 50 mph along the coast and 40 mph inland. The most significant effects are expected to impact the mid-Atlantic and Northeast, so be sure to check the weather forecast in your area before making your elderly grandparents brave treacherous roads.

West Coast travelers should be aware of the impact of potentially record-high king tides as well as a storm that's expected to bring rain, high-elevation snow, and dense fog from San Francisco all the way up the coast to Southern Washington. This king tide is expected to amplify the already elevated sea levels that have been affecting the West Coast thanks to the Super El Niño's higher water temperatures, potentially causing a surge of more than eight feet in San Francisco Bay. Waves are also expected to become dangerously large, reaching sizes of 20 to 30 feet on Wednesday. Federal experts say San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK), two of the largest airports in California's populous Bay Area, will flood this week from the huge tides. If you've been looking for an excuse to avoid the holiday chaos and stay home to play more GTA, just blame the weather forecast and order takeout.

#5605. Toxic Port Pollution Costs Europe €2.5bn A Year In Health & Environmental Damages — Study

New research reveals a single ship emits, on average, as much toxic sulphur at port in a year as 19,300 cars, leaving taxpayers and hospitals to pay the hidden cost of shipping pollution.

Commercial ships docked in European ports inflict €2.5 billion a year in societal and environmental costs, according to new research by T&E. While upcoming EU port rules will cut at-berth damages by 40% by 2030, most vessels remain exempt. Previous research has shown that residents living close to a commercial harbour already face significantly higher risks of cardiovascular and respiratory mortality¹. Tightening port pollution rules would save society billions and protect the health of port communities, says T&E.

Instead of plugging into the electrical grid when they dock, thousands of commercial vessels run diesel generators around the clock to power onboard systems. These idling engines release harmful pollution directly into neighbouring coastal and port communities. Analysis of Europe’s 100 largest ports shows that Rotterdam is the most polluted with costs at €350 million, followed by Antwerp (€220 million), Marseille (€120 million), Hamburg (€120 million), and Genoa (€110 million).

According to the report, removing loopholes in the EU rules would save Europe €1.56bn in health and climate costs. Under current EU rules, outlined in the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), only large container ships, ferries and cruise ships are required to plug into dockside electricity sockets, meaning oil and gas tankers, bulk carriers, car carriers and other cargo ships are left out entirely. Requirements to connect should be progressively extended to all ship types in the upcoming review to cut emissions and grant ports the necessary long-term predictability.

Eloi Nordé, shipping policy officer at T&E, said: “Port communities are paying the price for ships running their engines 24/7 at port. Fossil fuels only seem cheap because companies offload health and climate costs onto the public. Fortunately, the solution already exists. Plugging ships into shoreside electric power would save society billions and make port cities far healthier to live in.”

On paper, marine fuels appear less costly than drawing electricity from the port grid. However, this is largely because the associated healthcare and environmental burdens are absorbed by the local population rather than ship operators. Once these external costs are factored into energy pricing, generating power from fossil fuels at dock is twice as costly as using shore electricity.

This policy gap creates a lot of planning uncertainty for EU port authorities and electricity grid operators. Without a predictable policy progressively including all vessel types, ports are disincentivised from making long-term investments in green infrastructure, says T&E.

The EU will review the regulation at the end of this year. T&E urges EU policymakers to use the AFIR review to expand shore power to all ships, batteries, and boilers, backed by national port electrification roadmaps before 2032.

Its call is echoed today in a joint letter to the European Commission from the Clean Port Cities (CPC) coalition, uniting industry, civil society, and maritime and energy stakeholders including DFDS and Green Transition Denmark, urging predictable shore power timelines for all vessels, battery charging rules, and faster grid access.

¹ The port-health research cited refers to Mei et al. (2023), “Long-term effects of air pollutants on respiratory and cardiovascular mortality in a port city along the Adriatic sea,” BMC Pulmonary Medicine.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

#5604. Rare Muscle Disease Gets Its First Approved Therapy

— FDA approved ribitol to treat limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9

The FDA approved ribitol (Welgemda), an oral small molecule, to treat limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9 (LGMD2I/R9) in adults and children weighing at least 30 kg, the agency said Monday.

The treatment is the first therapy approved for any form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, the FDA noted.

"Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is a progressive muscle disease that gradually takes away a patient's ability to walk, breathe, and live independently, often beginning in childhood," said Laura Jawidzik, MD, of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. "The clinical data supporting Welgemda's approval show meaningful improvements in walking speed and lung function, and we are encouraged by what that can mean for patients' daily lives."

LGMD2I/R9 is caused by mutations in the FKRP gene. In healthy individuals, the FKRP enzyme helps attach sugar molecules to alpha-dystroglycan to connect muscle cells with surrounding tissue. Ribitol is a naturally occurring, five-carbon sugar alcohol that may help support the glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan.

Clinical manifestations of LGMD2I/R9 include skeletal myopathy affecting the lower and then upper limbs, often accompanied by subsequent pulmonary muscle and cardiac muscle involvement.

The FDA's decision to approve ribitol was based on key measures from a planned interim analysis of data from the phase III FORTIFY trial, according to drugmaker BridgeBio. At 12 months:

"Families living with LGMD2I/R9 have never had disease-specific treatment and only had supportive care to manage progression," Matthew Wicklund, MD, of the University of Texas at San Antonio Health Science Center, said in the drugmaker's news release. "What we saw in FORTIFY was different: individuals became measurably better at the things that matter most day to day, including breathing easier, walking faster, walking farther, and less fatigue."

The double-blind FORTIFY trial randomized 112 patients with genetically confirmed LGMD2I/R9 to either twice-daily oral ribitol dissolved in water or to placebo for up to 36 months. Participants were 12 to 60 years old.

The most common adverse reactions included gastrointestinal effects (e.g., diarrhea or stomach pain) and joint pain, the FDA noted. Patients treated with ribitol showed significant increases in glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan, indicating the drug reached its intended target.

With the FDA's approval, BridgeBio plans to transition FORTIFY participants in the U.S. to an ongoing open-label extension study. Trial sites outside the U.S. will continue the trial as planned until each participant completes 36 months of treatment.

Ribitol is not approved or available in any other market. BridgeBio anticipates an immediate U.S. launch.

#5603. 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda For Sale With 58,000 Miles Shown Is Racing Royalty With A Wild History

Special is subjective — even when it comes to cars. A car that is special to you might just be junk to somebody else. Sorry to burst your bubble, but not every car can count itself among the unicorns and truly special automotive special editions. Then again, other cars are special, full stop. Cars with the sort of presence that makes the little hairs on the back of your neck stand at attention. Understandably, most of us don't often get to see such cars, like the Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda. Big V8 power and an even bigger personality quickly established the short-lived E-Body Hemi 'Cuda as a muscle car mainstay.

Every once in a great while, one of these special Mopar muscle cars comes up for sale. But seldom does one with this sort of record head to the auction block. This is not a Hollywood car, nor was it celebrity-owned. No, this 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda has a racing rap sheet longer than your arm, teeming with victories and championship wins. Better yet, the 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8-powered racing legend racked up its impressive record as a primary factory-backed race car for Ecurie Chrysler in France, of all places. This is one well-traveled 'Cuda. Now, the esteemed asphalt-kicking American ambassador and its 58,000-mile odometer are back in the U.S. of A. and up for grabs courtesy of Bring a Trailer.

You might not expect a 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda to rack up race wins in France, but this 'Cuda did just that. Henri Chemin, the Chrysler France competition director at the time, drove the car in many Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) and Fédération Française du Sport Automobile (FFSA) events. Chemin managed nine victories in 1970, 16 wins in 1971, and seven victories in 1972. Jean-François Mas took the wheel in 1973, winning 12 times in 1973. This Hemi 'Cuda's last recorded victory was the handiwork of Jean-Claude Géral, who drove the muscle car to victory at the 1974 hillclimb event in Charnizay. All said and done, the 'Cuda claimed 45 Group 1 wins and three FIA championships between 1970 and 1974.

So, what state is the car in today? For starters, the restored-and-retired racer packs a 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8. That Hemi replaced the 'Cuda's original mill during the 1971 season. Should the next owner want to set up a display, the sale includes the original engine block, as well as extensive documentation, photos, a Simca en Compétition racing book, and Chemin's press clippings. A Hurst pistol-grip shifter commands the 'Cuda's four-speed manual transmission, while a Shaker hood and air dam help the old Mopar look the part.

In keeping with its racing DNA, the old Plymouth features a roll cage, Simpson harnesses, and a white-and-blue racing livery. Other features include 15" Rally wheels in a complementary white hue, body-colored bumpers, front disc brakes, a wood-rimmed steering wheel, an ATL fuel cell, and a dual exhaust system with Flowmaster mufflers.

We don't have to tell you that racing is dangerous — for both driver and machine. Duh, right? Well, at the Brides–Méribel hillclimb event in 1970, the Ecurie Chrysler Hemi 'Cuda met with a motorsport disaster of its own. Piloted by Chemin, the 'Cuda's power steering failed, causing the car to crash into a ravine. The crash was as bad as it sounds. Ecurie Chrysler deemed the Plymouth's body shell beyond repair. So, the racing team's engineers and mechanics salvaged everything they could, including the original engine, much of the drivetrain, the gauges, and the seats. They then transplanted it all into a replacement E-body from a 440 Six-Pack 'Cuda that Chemin had brought into France with the original factory-backed car.

Want this one? You're going to pay for it. As of this writing, the high bid for the Ex-Ecurie Chrysler France 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda is $110,000. Now, stock and well-preserved Hemi 'Cudas routinely net six-figure sums when they go up for sale. Don't believe it? This 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda with 31,300 miles that we reported on last month sold for $176,000 on Mecum. Add a factory convertible configuration into the mix, and a third-gen Hemi 'Cuda has the potential to cross the block for seven figures. After all, just 12 factory rag-top Hemi 'Cudas rolled off the line as 1971 models, making the classic Plymouth a 'Holy Grail' of muscle cars.

There's plenty of space for this motorsport Mopar to sell for big bucks. We just hope someone buys this tenured racing machine and lets it off its leash from time to time. It would be a shame for this one to spend too much time locked away from view with an odometer reading under 60,000 miles.

#5602. GLP-1 Use Linked to Increased Breast Density on Mammograms

— Majority of patients had increases in breast density but cancer risk implications remain unclear

Weight loss associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists may alter breast density on mammography, potentially complicating interpretation of the images, an analysis involving more than 100 patients suggested.

Mammographic breast density by automated assessment increased by at least one category in almost two-thirds of patients after a year of treatment with a GLP-1 agonist. None of the automated assessments showed a decline in breast density. Greater weight loss had a modest association with greater increases in automated breast-density assessment. Density-change assessments varied among three radiologists who reviewed each mammogram.

About a fifth of the patients had recalls for additional assessment (at least twice the national average), and four underwent breast biopsies, all of which proved to be negative, according to Eva C. Gombos, MD, of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston. She will report the study at the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) meeting, which begins Nov. 29 in Chicago.

"The findings do not suggest that patients should be concerned about taking GLP-1 medications," Gombos said in an RSNA press release. "An increase in mammographic density after substantial weight loss does not necessarily mean that the amount of fibroglandular tissue has increased or that breast cancer risk has increased. The long-term risk implications of these imaging changes remain uncertain and require further study. However, substantial weight loss may change the mammographic appearance of the breast, which could lead to additional imaging or a screening callback."

Women taking GLP-1 receptor agonists should continue routine breast cancer screening according to existing recommendations, she added.

Changes in breast density after weight loss are not a new observation, but they have become more common with the growing use of GLP-1 drugs, said Joseph Villavicencio, MD, of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, who was not involved in the study. A recent case review that he co-authored showed that "breast imaging findings following the use of GLP-1 agonists may vary, including both significant and insignificant increases in breast density. Patients with increased breast density may warrant further evaluation with supplemental screening."

"There is published data that increased breast density has been associated with an increased risk of breast cancer," Villavicencio told MedPage Today. "It's not clear that it applies to this situation."

A study reported at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology meeting suggested the opposite effect, as patients treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists had a 25% lower breast cancer risk, he added. Another study reported at the meeting showed that GLP-1 agonist users had a significantly lower risk of progression in four different types of cancer, including breast cancer.

"I think the implication really is that we may need patients to come back after screening -- patients who previously didn't require supplemental screening -- as their breast density changes," said Villavicencio.

"The [current] study mentions that contextualizing information is important, and I think that's extremely helpful," he added. "There are different reasons for changes in breast density, and knowing what's causing it can help us understand if this is something that's worrisome or not."

Gombos and colleagues performed a retrospective longitudinal analysis to investigate within-patient changes in mammographic breast density after GLP-1 receptor agonist-associated weight loss. Additionally, they examined the relationship between magnitude of weight loss and breast density changes, associated mammographic findings, and impact on recall rates.

The 107 patients had a mean age of 57.5 and had mammograms before starting GLP-1 agonists and at least 1 year afterward. Changes in breast density were assessed by an automated software program and by three breast radiologists. Using American College of Radiology BI-RADS criteria, the radiologists assessed breast density categories, subjective changes in density, breast size change, and skin thickening.

By automated analysis, 65 of 104 (62.5%) patients had an increase in breast density. Most of the patients (57 of 64) had one-category increases, and the remaining eight had two-category increases. No patient had a decrease in breast density by automated analysis.

A 30-lb median weight loss was associated with no change in breast density, whereas a 38-lb loss was associated with a one-category increase and 40 lb with a two-category increase, resulting in a modest association between weight loss and automated density-category increase (P=0.0366).

Visual assessment by the radiologists varied, as reader-specific decreases in breast size ranged from 57.9% to 78.5% and magnitude of skin thickening from 9.3% to 17.8%.

The screening recall rate was 22.4% (24 of 107 women). According to the American Cancer Society, the national recall rate averages about 10%, and the American College of Radiology has a target range of 5-12%. Gombos noted that the technical recall rate, unrelated to a suspicious finding, was 1.9%.

#5600. Slate Thinks 205 Miles Is More Than Enough Range

Slate Auto is in a strange spot. Yes, with a starting price of $26,400, including destination, the two-door pickup truck it's selling is cheap compared to the competition, but it also lacks basic features like power windows and a radio at that price. With options that'll make the truck more livable for everyday use, prices will quickly climb. No matter which options they choose, they'll still be saddled with the same 205 miles of range. Even though that's quite meager by today's standards, Slate feels that's more than enough to win over customers.

It makes sense why the Slate has such a shoddy range, even compared to its competition. The battery is the single most expensive part of an electric vehicle, so an automaker looking to make a cheap EV will use a smaller battery. There's a view that Slate's approach could work for folks who are already comfortable with EVs, but it might not translate for those more accustomed to what gas-powered vehicles offer, according to Automotive News. There's also the issue that similarly priced rivals will offer more range on base models, and they usually have the option of extended-range batteries.

Still, Slate feels 205 miles is really all the average American needs from a vehicle like its truck, the cheapest EV and pickup for sale in the U.S. To be fair, it's also the smallest pickup in the U.S. — about two feet shorter than a Ford Maverick. In a marketing email sent earlier this month, Slate said 205 miles is "more than [many people] need each day." That's sort of fair, because according to a 2024 survey done by AAA, the average American drives about 31 miles per day, meaning that from full to empty, you'd only need to charge the Slate about once a week. Of course, no one actually drives like that, and the range will never actually be 205 miles, but we can't really account for that.

Slate isn't the only company offering an EV with less-than-stellar range. The Kia EV3 compact crossover, which starts at $31,385, comes as standard with 221 miles of range. While the starting prices are far different, the EV3 comes with a lot more from the get-go. To get the Slate to a comparable place, you've got to add a bed kit that brings in seats and a roof — giving the Slate "crossover" a $31,400 base price, according to AutoNews. It'll still be missing plenty of other things at that price, like a radio and electric windows.

In any case, Kia doesn't expect this low-range EV3 to be a big seller — capturing just 3 to 5% of its sales. The higher Wind trim, with its 321 miles of range and $36,485 starting price, is expected to be the volume seller with about 60% of sales. That sort of speaks to Slate's problem. It seems like folks would rather pay the extra money to not have to worry about range anxiety or charging up their cars as often.

In reality, the EV3 isn't a direct competitor to the Slate, but Ford's yet-to-be-unveiled Fathom pickup is. It's expected to have a standard battery with around 250 miles of range and an optional battery with over 300 miles, Automotive News reports. Despite the fact it range-mogs the Slate, its starting price will come in at $29,945, including shipping, and it'll be an actual vehicle with the sort of modern luxuries and conveniences you'd expect in today's day and age.

I'm not saying that the Slate is dead on arrival by any means, but I do think the Jeff Bezos-backed company is really, really hoping that there are a lot of Quirked Up Individuals out there who will fall for the proletariat virtual signals of crank windows, no radio, a key you've got to insert and no screen while also paying a price that doesn't really connect with that reality. I'm not sure they're out there.

#5599. Rotterdam’s Methanol Expansion Is Not an Inland Shipping Fuel Strategy

Rotterdam is expanding its methanol and ethanol business for industrial customers and ocean-going ships. Its inland freight fleet needs a different energy strategy. Confusing cargo, marine bunkering and propulsion would commit port authorities to parallel fuel networks when regular freight routes offer a stronger case for direct electrification.

In May 2026, Tankmatch’s inland bunker vessel MTS Experience delivered certified biomethanol and second-generation ethanol to X-Press Feeders’ ocean-going Eco Levant. The fuels were transferred separately and blended aboard the receiving ship into 90% methanol and 10% ethanol. It was Rotterdam’s first ethanol bunkering of a seagoing vessel. The receiving ship burned the alcohol blend. The inland barge delivered it as cargo. Those are two different businesses.

Rotterdam had already announced an expansion of Evos’s Europoort terminal. Five storage tanks totaling 67,500 m³ are planned for methanol and ethanol, along with an inland-shipping berth scheduled for completion in early 2028. The berth includes shore power for vessels alongside. The project expands industrial storage, cargo transshipment and marine bunkering capacity. Developing an electric inland-freight corridor requires a separate charging and battery-service plan.

Low-carbon alcohols have a role in shipping services that still need liquid fuel. Aviation competes for oils and fats suitable for renewable diesel, leaving other sustainable feedstocks for marine alcohol fuels. I reassessed biomethanol’s role in the residual liquid-fuel market and examined alcohol-fuel generators as range extenders for hybrid ships. The investment test is lifecycle emissions, delivered fuel cost and demand from ships that need liquid energy.

The five planned tanks add 67,500 m³ of storage capacity across several markets. Rotterdam’s biomethanol bunkering grew from about 3,900 tons to almost 12,000 tons in 2025, according to the port authority. That is growth from a small base in the wider bunker market. Long-term investment still depends on recurring customers, contracted volumes and infrastructure utilization.

Ocean-going ships arrive with different engines, fuel contracts and routes. International ports will serve several bunker fuels for years. Los Angeles and Long Beach are approaching this market in stages, beginning with the fuels visiting vessels can buy and the commercial commitments needed for expansion. My assessment of those ports makes the same distinction between proving safe delivery and proving repeatable demand.

Inland shipping is a separate energy business. Many freight routes repeat between a limited number of ports and terminals. Charging equipment, onboard storage and battery exchange can follow sailing schedules, cargo cycles and terminal availability. A shared electrical network can serve dry cargo barges, chemical tankers and container vessels with different battery configurations and common interfaces.

My 98-page inland freight electrification report models five complete loaded-and-empty route cycles. A local port-canal shuttle requires 1.8 MWh, regional industrial service 4.3 MWh, irregular service 8.3 MWh, a major-port corridor 13.1 MWh and a long industrial corridor 36.8 MWh. These planning values precede vessel design margins. The twentyfold spread calls for different battery sizes, exchange frequencies and charging arrangements within a common electric propulsion system.

Some predictable services can charge fixed batteries during normal stops. Others benefit from exchangeable 20-foot battery containers, with smaller onboard batteries supplying hotel loads and resilience. Long corridors need reliable intermediate energy points. Hazardous-cargo tankers need cargo-pump integration, electrical segregation, fire protection and appropriate approvals. Those are problems of vessel design, safety approval and electrical infrastructure. Adding hydrogen, LNG and methanol supply chains adds costs of its own.

The Dutch Zero Emission Services model is already operating at modest scale. It lists five charging stations, two vessels in service and twelve conversion subsidies. Battery-container ownership and energy service can be separated from vessel ownership. Its shared interfaces demonstrate how multiple operators can purchase energy service from the same battery and charging network.

The Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine records battery, hydrogen and LNG vessels, then argues that inland navigation has no universal propulsion solution. Its selected deployment database includes passenger vessels as well as freight. That inventory tells us which technologies have been tried. Comparing their economics and infrastructure costs is a separate task. Inland fleets can use varied hulls, battery sizes and charging arrangements while converging on electricity as the main propulsion energy carrier.

Port authorities need three distinct investment cases. Industrial alcohol storage needs chemical customers and cargo commitments. Marine bunkering needs ocean-going ship demand, fuel certification and contracts. Inland propulsion needs route-by-route electricity requirements, grid connections, terminal windows and a dependable energy service. Sharing port land and utilities can lower costs. Confusing the three markets can multiply them.

Rotterdam can expand methanol and ethanol handling while building a common electric backbone for inland freight. The barge carrying methanol does not need to burn it. Port investment should follow the service purchased by each customer.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Rotterdam’s three energy businesses, the different inland route requirements and the investment implications. The supporting 98-page report contains the route energy and vessel architecture analysis.

#5598. New York Just Banned Subscriptions For Features Your Car Already Has

In-vehicle subscriptions are pretty universally maligned among car owners. Most folks don't like the feeling of having to pay every month for features their cars were supposed to come with, and now New York State is doing something about it. Governor Kathy Hochul just signed a bill that bars automakers, dealers and their agents from selling subscriptions for features that are already installed.

The new law, which takes effect on February 27, 2027, is part of a new section of the state's General Business Law, according to Spectrum News. You can read the law for yourself here. It lays out fairly simple ground rules when it comes to subscriptions dealers or manufacturers can offer you: The feature must use hardware already in the car when it was bought or leased, and it must keep working without continual costs or support from the automaker or a third party. Those two things pretty much bring an end to crap like subscription-based heated seats and alike. It also is supposed to cover hands-off driving systems and enhanced navigation. Basically, once the hardware is physically in the car and the manufacturer isn't paying anything for you to use it, they can't then charge you. OEMs will also not be able to charge for software updates that fix safety defects.

Hochul called the practice a "deceptive business model," according to CBS 6 Albany. She also told automakers to keep their hands out of New Yorkers' wallets. It passed through the New York State Senate 57-3.

As with all good things, there are some exceptions. First of all, your lease or payment plan doesn't count as a subscription, so don't even try it, slick.

The law also doesn't apply to navigation updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle WiFi, telematics, roadside assistance or "vehicle-connected services" that rely on cellular data or other networks, according to Motor1. It also exempts software-dependent driver assistance features, like Tesla's Full Self-Driving or GM's Super Cruise.

I know what you're thinking. Didn't I just mention that hands-free driving systems are covered? Well, yes, but subscriptions tied to software and data are likely to survive, while hardware-only features are the real targets. Automakers will almost certainly make the argument that things like FSD and Super Cruise are "connected" or "software-dependent."

One prime example of what this bill aims to get rid of is BMW keeping things like a 360-degree camera behind a paywall. That hardware is already built into the car, and, as we reported, it doesn't require a data connection to operate. It's the same thing with features like high-beam assist and remote start, so I imagine it'll be hard for BMW and other companies with similar schemes to argue that these are "connected." I mean, these are the same people who argue that buyers actually want subscriptions, which is certainly not true.

In any case, violators will face civil penalties of up to $250 per point-of-sale for each violation, though it's not clear exactly how that'll be counted. It's not clear if other states are going to follow suit, but here's hoping.

#5597. Pro-Abortion Rights Dems Won Big in the Election, but Vast Changes Are Unlikely Soon

— Democrats failed to take full control in states where laws are strictest

Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government offices. But it's not likely that they'll be able to impose quick and vast abortion policy changes.

That's because Democrats did not take full control of the legislatures and governor's offices in states with the strictest laws -- those that ban abortion at 6 weeks or all stages of pregnancy.

And in Congress, Democrats who will control both the House and Senate could attempt to bar states from adopting some kinds of abortion bans, but any move would likely meet a veto from President Donald Trump, which couldn't be overridden without GOP help.

Officials in Two States Are Calling for Constitutional Protections for Abortion

Abortion has been primarily a state government issue since the U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 ruling that struck down Roe v. Wade allowed states to enforce bans. Now, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy -- with some exceptions -- and four more do so after about the first 6 weeks.

In 2027, Democrats will have control of both legislative chambers and the governor's office in six states where they currently share power with Republicans. Those states -- Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin -- already allow abortion until at least fetal viability, which is generally considered to be sometime after 21 weeks of pregnancy.

Abortion is currently allowed through the first 20 weeks from fertilization, or about 22 weeks' gestation in Wisconsin and 23 weeks in Pennsylvania. Democrats kept the governorships and gained full power in the legislatures in the elections in both states.

Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are both calling for leveraging that power to amend their states' constitutions to create a right to abortion.

Voters in a dozen states already have passed similar amendments, including two -- Nevada and Virginia -- this year. Voters in November also kept such protections in Missouri but defeated an initiative to add them to state law in Idaho.

Georgia Democrats Could Attempt to Repeal a Ban

In Georgia, where Democrats gained the House and the governor's office, abortion is banned in most cases after fetal cardiac activity can be detected -- around 6 weeks into pregnancy and before many women realize they're pregnant.

Josh McLaurin, the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor, is optimistic that one Republican state senator would be willing to join Democrats to repeal that law.

The measure could get at least a vote in the Senate, he said, because Republicans will have a 29-27 majority and may not take a "hyper-partisan approach" to block it.

McLaurin said that voters see the ban as a healthcare issue, especially after a state review board in 2024 found that two women died in Georgia after doctors were hesitant to perform abortions that could have saved their lives.

Still, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms acknowledged that a GOP-held state Senate could be an obstacle.

"If we see a pathway to do something about it this session, then we're going to take that opportunity," Bottoms said at a news conference. "And it may not be this session."

A New Texas Attorney General Will End Some Legal Challenges

After winning the attorney general election in Texas, Democrat Nathan Johnson said he would not sue out-of-state medical providers who prescribe abortion pills via telehealth and ship them to patients in the state as the outgoing attorney general, Republican Ken Paxton, has done. Paxton dropped his suits in November.

Those pills often come from states that seek to protect medical professionals who prescribe them through telehealth and ship them to patients in places with bans. That practice is why the number of abortions has been higher since the fall of Roe. It's also the heart of the current abortion legal battles.

Johnson could also withdraw Texas from a lawsuit challenging federal policy on the abortion pill mifepristone and decide not to defend the state's abortion restrictions against lawsuits.

"It is deeply gutting that now we don't have Texas to be fighting with the pro-life side on this," said Kelsey Pritchard, spokesperson for SBA Pro-Life America.

Abortion Opponents Are Focused on Access to Pills

Pritchard and other anti-abortion activists are pushing the Trump administration to make mifepristone harder to get by persuading the FDA, which is studying the drug, to bar filling prescriptions through the mail or at pharmacies. The FDA has said it'll have more information by March.

They're also counting on remaining Republican state attorneys general to keep up the fight.

Ohio lawmakers this month passed legislation to bar telehealth prescriptions for mifepristone sent into the state and to reimpose a 24-hour waiting period before obtaining an abortion. It's not clear whether outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine will sign them into law -- or how courts would rule on legal challenges. Voters passed a constitutional amendment protecting abortion access in 2023.

Ingrid Duran, state legislative director at the National Right to Life Committee, said her group will keep pushing measures that Democrats sometimes support -- such as supporting ways for women to anonymously and safely give up newborns for adoption. And, she said, it will encourage anti-abortion bills that may not have much of a chance of passing now as a way to build for the future.

"We're not going to give up just because it's going to be more challenging," she said.

Republicans Still Control the White House

Some congressional Democrats are planning to push forward a measure that would bar states from banning abortion before viability and rescind restrictions that some states have -- such as requiring multiple doctor's visits or ultrasounds.

With a Trump veto expected if it reaches him, the effort would be aimed largely at forcing him to reject a policy that has public opinion on its side.

About 6 in 10 U.S. voters said abortion should be legal in all or most cases, according to the AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters in all 50 states.

#5596. 2027 Toyota Sienna Now Gets Up To 37 MPG Combined, And It'll Be Better To Drive Too

If you're still hating on minivans in The Year Of Our Lord 2026, the joke is officially on you. Minivans are exceptionally versatile vehicles that are objectively the best option for most modern SUV buyers, but their lack of a perceived cool factor prevents many buyers from even considering them. We love minivans, and one of the most compelling minivans on the market today is the hybrid-only Toyota Sienna. It's getting even more compelling for 2027, since Toyota has bestowed it with some significant drivetrain improvements including the automaker's sixth-generation hybrid system that uses high efficiency electric motors, a retuned engine, and a more energy efficient lithium-ion battery.

The 2027 Toyota Sienna isn't visibly distinguishable from the 2026 model since no changes were made to its exterior, but minivans have always been about what's beneath the skin, anyway. In addition to the new powertrain, all 2027 Siennas get the larger 12.3-inch infotainment screen and the larger 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster as standard, Toyota's latest suite of active-safety features, an integrated dash cam, a redesigned steering wheel and column, and new LED interior lights.

The Sienna's new hybrid powertrain has been totally recalibrated to operate the 2.5-liter four-cylinder at lower engine speeds when accelerating through the low and mid-range, and all Siennas now have a 1.15-kWh lithium-ion battery and a 166-horsepower electric motor. The powertrain produces a combined 251 horsepower, 6 more horses than last year, and Toyota reckons it's good for a 0.3-second quicker 0-to-60 sprint of 7.5 seconds in front-wheel-drive form. It can still be had with all-wheel drive, which adds a rear-mounted 54-hp electric motor, but its 0-to-60 time is actually a tenth slower than the front-drive model. Toyota now estimates both FWD and AWD Siennas will return 39 mpg in the city, 35 mpg on the highway, and 37 mpg combined, improvements of 3 mpg for FWD and 4 mpg for AWD.

Toyota says the new steering system is more direct and has better on-center feel while reducing steering effort at low speeds for easier parking thanks to a new steering gear box, motor control unit, and torque sensor. The Sienna's brakes have also been reworked with a new electronic control system, offering improved feel and response with less body roll. The latest Toyota Safety Sense 4.0 suite of active safety features has upgraded sensors and hardware for improved obstacle detection capabilities, and in case that all fails, a built-in dash cam comes standard.

Other little changes include the cancellation of the Limited model, now leaving base LE, XLE, Woodland, XSE, and top Platinum trim levels. Toyota has not yet release pricing for the updated 2027 Sienna, but we expect its prices to increase slightly from their current starting point of $42,915.

#5595. Post-quantum cryptography startup Q.security launches with $11.5M in funding

Post-quantum cryptography startup Q Security Inc. formally launched today with $11.5 million in new funding for a platform designed to take enterprises from discovery through to completion of their quantum-safe migrations.

Founded this year, Q.security offers a remediation platform that runs the move to post-quantum cryptography as one coordinated program. The company argues that security teams need business context to decide which cryptographic findings to address first, since the time and resources available for the work are limited.

At the core of the Q.security offering is a map of an organization’s business structure and applications. Findings from the cryptographic inventory are tied back to that map, with the highest-risk assets put at the front of the queue.

Teams are said to be able to investigate exposure and work through remediation using a conversational artificial intelligence interface. Through integrations with existing cybersecurity and infrastructure tools, the platform drives fixes to completion using AI-guided runbooks, ticketing and automation.

Once a fix is in place, Q.security verifies that it works. Monitoring of the organization’s cryptographic posture then continues as standards and threats change, an approach the company claims lets security teams reduce risk faster and at lower cost.

“Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Guy Peer, co-founder and chief executive of Q.security, who previously co-founded Unbound Security and led its research and development through its acquisition by Coinbase Global Inc., announced in 2021.

Peer’s co-founder, Nir Steinherz, was director of product at Coinbase and vice president of strategy and product at Unbound Security. He was also a senior vice president at Citigroup Inc.’s Security Innovation Center, where he led secure digital banking initiatives for more than 100 million customers. The pair are said to have led a cryptographic migration protecting hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.

The funding is intended to support Q.security as it brings its platform to enterprise customers through direct sales and channel partners.

Castle Island Ventures led the seed round, with New York Life Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund and Ground Up Ventures also participating.

Matt Walsh, general partner at Castle Island Ventures, said enterprises know they need to prepare for the day quantum computers can break current encryption. With harvest-now, decrypt-later data collection already under way, “the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments,” he added.

#5594. First Systemic Therapy for Nonsegmental Vitiligo Gets FDA Green Light

— Upadacitinib reduced facial and total body area affected by 40-50% at 76 weeks

The FDA has approved upadacitinib (Rinvoq) for nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV), the first systemic therapy approved for the condition.

The approval allows use of the JAK inhibitor in patients 12 years or older, according to an announcement from AbbVie. Other approved therapies, including JAK inhibitors, are topical and typically used to treat specific areas of skin depigmentation.

"For the vitiligo community, approval of the first systemic treatment option for nonsegmental vitiligo is an important development in advancing care," Richard Huggins, MD, of Henry Ford Health in Detroit, said in the announcement. "This approval reflects growing recognition of vitiligo as a serious autoimmune disease and the true burden it places on those living with the condition."

Principal support for the approval came from the phase III Viti-Up clinical program comprising two identically designed, randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving adults and adolescents with NSV. The co-primary endpoints in both trials were clinically meaningful improvement in facial repigmentation (F-VASI 75) and total body repigmentation (T-VASI 50) after 48 weeks.

The results showed that about a fourth of patients on the JAK inhibitor achieved F-VASI 75 at 48 weeks in both trials versus 6-7% of the placebo group. Rates of T-VASI 50 at 48 weeks were 20% with upadacitinib and 6% with placebo. After 76 weeks of follow-up, about half of upadacitinib-treated patients met F-VASI 75 criteria in the two studies combined, and 40-45% met T-VASI 50 response criteria.

"The Viti-Up clinical program is particularly impactful because it demonstrates the potential of a systemic treatment to achieve robust facial and total body repigmentation," said investigator Seemal Desai, MD, of Innovative Dermatology in Dallas and president of the Global Vitiligo Foundation. "We know that repigmentation takes time, and the significant improvements observed at week 76, with facial and total body response rates doubling or nearly doubling from week 48, are especially encouraging and reinforce the value of a treatment approach that targets the disease from within."

Neither clinical trial had reports of major adverse cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolic events, gastrointestinal perforations, active tuberculosis, lymphoma, non-melanoma skin cancer, or opportunistic infections other than herpes zoster. Overall, safety data were consistent with the known upadacitinib safety profile.

The recommended upadacitinib dose for NSV is 15 mg. The NSV indication adds to existing approvals for the JAK inhibitor that include rheumatoid arthritis, atopic dermatitis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, giant cell arteritis, ulcerative colitis, and Crohn's disease.
