#5593. Long Before The U.S. Air Force Existed, The Army Used Planes Made By The Wright Brothers

With how ubiquitous commercial air travel is today it's easy to overlook how astonishingly rapid early aircraft development was. There were only 24 years between the maiden flight of the Wright Flyer in 1903 and Charles Lindbergh made the first solo transatlantic flight in 1927. However, military thinkers were even quicker to realize the potential of powered flight on the battlefield. The U.S. Army purchased a Wright Military Flyer in 1909 for use as an observation aircraft. The first heavier-than-air military aircraft served as the spark that eventually led to creation of the U.S. Air Force, but it wasn't an unmitigated success.

The tactical advantage of holding the higher ground had been known for centuries, but aircraft opened up an entirely new dimension. Initially, it was hot air balloons taking to the wild blue yonder. During the Civil War, the Union Army fielded a balloon corps to perform reconnaissance and scout Confederate Army positions. The corps wouldn't last long with then-General Ulysses S. Grant dissolving the unit in August 1863.

The U.S. Army decided to revive this reconnaissance role when opening bidding for a two-seat observation aircraft in 1908. According to the U.S. Department of Defense, the Wright Military Flyer reached an altitude of 400 feet while averaging a speed of 42.5 miles per hour during its final ten-mile qualifying flight in July 1909. The service would purchase a single Wright Military Flyer for $30,000 next month. The sum would be $1.1 million today when adjusted for inflation.

The demonstration campaign that convinced the U.S. Army Signal Corps to open its checkbooks wasn't flawless. Orville Wright would bring a Wright Model A plane to Fort Myer near Arlington National Cemetery in 1908. The younger Wright brother flew dignitaries on brief flights around the Fort's drilling grounds in front of over 2,000 people.

The spectacle was going perfectly until First Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge climbed abroad as a passenger. He had been the first U.S. Army officer to fly a plane just months earlier. According to Air & Space Magazine, Model A suffered a propeller failure while flying at 40 mph at an altitude of at least 100 feet. The twin-propeller wood and canvas biplane tumbled out of control and plummeted to the ground. Wright was seriously injured, but the crash killed Selfridge.

In the crash's aftermath, a distraught Wright believed that he could've landed the plane safely if he had "a few feet more" of altitude. He returned to Fort Myer with an upgraded plane the next year and secured the sale to the Signal Corps. The Wright Military Flyer would never see combat, but it's easy to see how the early aircraft would've been vulnerable to machine gun fire from the ground with such a low maximum altitude. It wouldn't be the U.S. Army's last foray into experimental aircraft. The service would dabble in early drone warfare less than a decade later.

#5592. Can ctDNA Help Guide Treatment Decisions in Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer?

— Experts discuss new ESMO findings and the limits of risk stratification

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three expert leaders in the field of bladder cancer discuss the latest research presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress.

Moderator Matthew Galsky, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, is joined by David Aggen, MD, PhD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and Stephanie Berg, DO, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

In this third of four episodes, they examine new findings about circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from KEYNOTE-B15, as well as its potential for predicting recurrence and the unanswered questions about using ctDNA to guide treatment decisions.

Click here to watch all episodes of this roundtable series.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Galsky: So let's talk a little bit about the next topic, which is ctDNA. And we saw ctDNA all over the place at ESMO this year, including in some high-profile presentations related to large randomized studies. So we're really starting to get, one, more data in the context of randomized studies, and two, we're beginning to see some data with different strategies for testing ctDNA after having had data really limited to what I'll call the standard Signatera assay for a while.

So let's talk about some of that data. So we saw data from KEYNOTE-B15, and remember KEYNOTE-B15 enrolled patients who were cisplatin-ineligible* with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, and patients were randomized to receive perioperative EV [enfortumab vedotin (Padcev)], pembro [pembrolizumab (Keytruda)], and cystectomy versus neoadjuvant gem-cis [gemcitabine and cisplatin] and cystectomy; ctDNA testing was done with the Signatera assay using the more standard approach in that study.And on the EV-pembro arm, there was an 82% rate of clearance of ctDNA from baseline to pre-cystectomy versus 66.7% with neoadjuvant gem-cis. [*Editor's note: KEYNOTE-B15 enrolled cisplatin-eligible patients.]

And presurgical ctDNA negativity did not absolutely predict a path CR [pathological complete response], but it was associated with a higher path CR rate and certainly was associated with more favorable event-free survival. We saw that in the post-cystectomy setting, the likelihood of having detectable ctDNA with modern treatment regimens and cystectomy was really pretty minuscule, in about the 5% range post-cystectomy. So Dr. Aggen, what do you make of that data and how do you use it in clinic?

Aggen: So I think it's exciting now that with a more sensitive whole-genome-based assay, 83% of patients pre-cystectomy are clearing their ctDNA. But the takeaway for me actually relates more to the other group that was positive pre-cystectomy. Even if they clear with surgery, that group is probably at a much higher risk of metastatic recurrence.

And so it does inform, for me, a patient with a positive ctDNA test before surgery is a patient who probably should be getting more adjuvant therapy. And so I think largely ctDNA in this setting is prognostic. We're trying to do the trials through Alliance to figure out if we can use that as a risk stratifier for those who have persistent positivity.

I think the other takeaway for me though, is that a negative test also doesn't mean that you're totally out of the woods. In the breakdown they showed by ctDNA status, the event-free survival at 2 years in the ctDNA-negative group was about 85 or 86%. So there's still a 15% chance that those patients recur.

So I think it's nice that we have this tool now for prognostication. I don't think it's quite there yet for how we risk stratify and it's not necessarily helping me to make a decision at this moment to deescalate therapy for patients.

Galsky: How about you, Dr. Berg? How do you use it? Is baseline ctDNA testing in muscle-invasive bladder cancer helpful? Does it help you decide who should get neoadjuvant treatment at all?

Berg: I do think so in the sense that when I think about ctDNA, and at least for perioperative therapy, you have your baseline, and then you have your post-treatment before surgery, and then you have your after treatment, and then you think about adjuvant treatment.

So a lot of the data, like Dr. Aggen was saying about being prognostic, is the patients that are just negative in the beginning at that first baseline test, they are doing very, very, very well. Going through the therapy, staying negative, having a good, probably, response, and then hopefully staying negative after that. Those patients we know we do well.

And I would emphasize, like Dr. Aggen was saying, if you're going into surgery still positive, that is something I think we can educate our patients really importantly about what that could mean, not to sway them away from potentially a curative surgery, but can have that discussion and then really follow it afterwards.

So I think it's really adding this extra layer for our conversations, probably can cause some anxiety and a lot more questions, but I think it's something that we are really building into our paradigm when we see our patients next to us and follow this real-time tracker with them. And it's exciting in a way, but also again, can make everyone feel very anxious. So I think when trials are coming in, we're going to really use that more.

And I know for your study, Dr. Galsky, how do we determine afterwards what we're doing with it? And do you need more if you're positive afterwards or can you go and have deescalate when you're negative? And what does that mean to be negative and stay negative, or positive to negative or negative to positive? It's a lot. It's a lot, but it's great to see all the data coming out and all the work being done in our large studies really adding that to the data. It really is, I think, so helpful for all of us because we all are using it so often in clinic.

Galsky: And we're just starting to scratch the surface regarding kinetics of change. So pre-cystectomy ctDNA detectability, like Dr. Aggen pointed out, it's probably not all created equally. And there are patients who are detectable prior to surgery who have a rising value. There are patients who are detectable prior to surgery having a declining value. And all of that probably matters somewhat, but we don't know how yet.

#5591. Here's What I Learned After Administering Naloxone

— Comprehensive overdose education goes beyond just giving the drug

In my first year of college, I saw a man drifting out of consciousness at a city intersection. His breathing was slow, and his lips were blue. The New Haven winter nipped relentlessly at exposed skin, and part of me suspected hypothermia. But after a sternal rub failed to wake him, I administered the naloxone (Narcan) I had made a habit of carrying and used a CPR mask to deliver rescue breaths. Within minutes, he regained consciousness. As I reached for my phone to call a friend to bring water, the man said, "Please don't call the police. I'd love somebody to just sit with me."

Darman* was unhoused and an Afghanistan veteran living with post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). There are parts of his story that I may never fully grasp, even now as a medical student -- or even after a decade as a physician. What I did understand was the importance of having someone to lean on and seeing the full human beyond his emergency.

This year, my classmates in student government and I worked with faculty at Stanford University School of Medicine to make opioid overdose training a required part of the curriculum for every incoming class of medical and physician assistant students. Substance use curriculum in medical schools has historically focused on alcohol and tobacco, and a 2024 systematic review of 192 institutions found that only 9.4% had opioid use disorder training programs.

We also recruited an instructor with lived experience of substance use to lead the course. This is part of a larger point my peers and I hope to make: every medical trainee should graduate prepared to reverse an overdose and approach substance use without judgment.

The opioid epidemic was declared a public health emergency in October 2017, and has since claimed half a million American lives. Its earlier waves were driven by prescription opioids and then heroin; a third wave began around 2013, with substantial increases in deaths involving synthetic opioids, particularly illicitly manufactured fentanyl and its analogs. From 1999 through 2023, approximately 806,000 people died from opioid overdoses. Deaths have declined in recent years, with supply-side changes and community prevention efforts among likely contributors.

However, now is not the time to take our feet off the pedals. The opioid crisis is ongoing, and certain regions of the U.S. continue to be impacted disproportionately. Alongside upstream governmental policies and campaigns, medical schools therefore have a responsibility to continue the grassroots work of educating the next generation of clinicians. Institutions should work alongside students to integrate overdose-response training throughout the curriculum, ensuring that this education remains a sustained commitment rather than relying on individual student initiatives to carry it forward.

However, simply distributing harm reduction supplies, such as naloxone, is not enough. When the conversation stops at naloxone, we leave out education on what to do while the medication takes effect and how to care for the person when they regain consciousness. Comprehensive overdose education must address both. Opioids depress the central nervous system, slowing or stopping breathing and depriving vital organs of oxygen. Naloxone blocks opioids' effects at their receptors and can restore breathing within several minutes. In the meantime, responders need to know how to support breathing to help prevent brain injury.

At our training, students practiced on CPR manikins: opening the airway by gently tilting the head back and lifting the chin, creating a secure seal with a CPR mask to reduce mouth-to-mouth contact, performing breaths, and monitoring the chest. Current American Heart Association guidance recommends one rescue breath every 6 seconds for an adult who has a pulse but is not breathing normally; if a pulse cannot be confirmed, CPR is needed. Students should also learn to stay with the person until emergency help arrives. Naloxone can precipitate severe withdrawal, and the effects of some opioids such as fentanyl can outlive the medication, making additional doses necessary.

Following their training at Stanford Medicine, every student now receives a free naloxone kit and a CPR breathing mask. We also recently worked with a campus center to install a harm reduction dispenser at the medical school. Successfully responding to an overdose depends in part on having these supplies close and accessible.

As students, we become part of the community where we go to school. We drink coffee in its neighborhoods, walk its streets, shop in its stores, read on its park benches. For a few years, we make a life there. The people who share this community with us become our neighbors, including the ones whose lives rarely intersect with ours inside the university. Preparing to care for them is part of belonging to a place.

That night, I stayed with Darman in a park while he recovered before asking permission to bring him to Yale-New Haven Hospital. Medical training, I learned, does not make us immune to homelessness, addiction, illness, or loss. He and I, you and me, we are bound by humanity and separated by circumstance. Darman and I both liked hot coffee and video games. He was a father; I hoped to become one someday. We both tried to speak to our mothers as often as we could -- I over the phone, he in prayer.

Medical training will teach us to move quickly, to make decisions under pressure, to find the next thing that needs doing. I hope we also learn to recognize when someone needs us as a shoulder. Every medical school should prepare its students for that responsibility, and we can start by supporting one of America's most vulnerable populations: victims of the opioid epidemic.

Looking back on my 4 years at Yale, I think of that night with Darman as the first time I felt like a true New Havener. For a little while, in the winter cold, we had each other. Today, as a medical student 3,000 miles away in California, in a place I am still learning to call home, that moment reminds me time and again that it is love -- the action -- not necessarily love, the loud, or love, the promised, that makes this life worth living and trying for.

#5590. Bootstrapped startup Levenza brings consumer-style personal agents to business workers

Artificial intelligence enthusiasts are embracing personal agents that can automate life’s most tedious digital chores, but office workers are still stuck juggling calendars, email messages and chat threads.

Levenza wants to change that with the launch of what it says are the first personal AI agents designed for corporate employees. The startup today announced the general availability of its enterprise-grade personal agents, together with its first acquisition in the shape of the AI research lab Fluid Inference.

In the last few months, personal AI agents have emerged as the hottest new trend in AI, sparking fierce competition among both technology giants and agentic startups. The biggest name is probably Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse, a “secure by design” personal assistant that quickly shot to the top of U.S. app charts following its launch in September. We’ve also seen OpenAI’s Dots, powered by GPT-6 Astra, which aim to proactively get work done on behalf of their users, as well as startups such as Instinct, which raised a colossal $1 billion in funding in September for its consumer-focused agents.

AI agents may still be somewhat divisive, but the early success of Muse, Dots and Instinct shows that there’s clearly a large market for automated assistants. Yet those tools are all targeted primarily at consumers rather than enterprise workers, which means there’s a massive gap in the market that’s waiting to be filled. Levenza wants to be the one that fills it, with its personal agents developed specifically to run inside sensitive corporate environments.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Haefa Mansour (pictured, left) told SiliconANGLE that the difference between Levenza’s agents and those of its competitors is that it takes time to work with individual companies to customize what they can and can’t do. She explained that workplace agents can only provide value if they’re able to connect to corporate systems securely and respect a company’s dynamics and security policies.

“People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside of work, and they’re expecting the same experience inside the office,” Mansour said. “But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, cha50sing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work.”

Levenza’s personal agents are designed to live inside of the platforms where work gets done, such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Slack. Within those environments, they act as proactive digital assistants for senior executives and other professionals.

Among other things, they can coordinate meetings across time zones, book hotel rooms, liaise with travel agencies, submit timesheets, triage overflowing email inboxes and send out replies and follow-ups when necessary. The more they do this work, the more they learn about the individual worker they’re serving, allowing them to become more useful over time, Mansour said.

By automating and coordinating routine work, Levenza’s agents can free workers from the “administrative drag” that affects every worker, slowing down productivity. “Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index found that the average worker receives 117 emails per day and is interrupted every two minutes,” Mansour said. “On top of the inbox and the calendar come the travel, expenses and follow-ups that slip through the cracks – none of this is work that professionals were actually hired to do.”

Mansour, a former Bain & Co. alumni who holds a Ph.D. from the University of California, founded Levenza alongside former Databricks Inc. and Uber Technologies Inc. engineer Austin Tackaberry (right) specifically to eliminate these distractions. The startup has made impressive traction, and despite not raising a dime in outside funding, its personal agents are already up and running at more than 300 enterprise customers, serving more than 10,000 professionals at those customers.

Early adopters such as Hg Capital and Oliver Wyman LLC report that their employees are saving up to three hours daily by offloading mundane admin to Levenza’s personal agents. They can also deal with any problems that occur during someone’s day. “For instance, if a manager’s customer workshop is running late and they’re likely to miss their flight, they don’t need to worry,” Mansour said. “Levenza will reach out to the travel management company to rebook according to their updated schedule.”

This means the manager in question will be able to focus on the workshop, safe in the knowledge that they’ll still be able to get to where they need to go after it does finish.

The acquisition of Fluid Inference is all about making Levenza’s agents more accessible. Mansour said the startup is an open-source research lab that’s focused on developing AI speech and ambient intelligence models.

By buying it, Levenza will be able to integrate natural voice interactions with its agents, so workers won’t have to tell them what needs to be done. Fluid Inference’s founder Brandon Weng is going to stick around as Levenza’s new head of engineering, adding much-needed talent to its team.

With Levenza’s agents now generally available, Mansour says the company will use its growing revenues to expand its third-party integrations and develop more capabilities for them. The company plans to launch automations for travel booking and expense management early next year, but that’s just the beginning.

“In the future, Levenza agents will operate with full autonomy in the enterprise, proactively deciding what work needs to be done,” she said. “They’ll coordinate with groups of other Levenza agents to collectively accomplish tasks.”

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

#5588. HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers roll out peptide offerings

HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers roll out peptide offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Direct-to-consumer health companies Noom and Hims & Hers are making a play for the peptide market as the federal government loosens restrictions on compounded treatments.

The companies are betting that peptides could be the next big thing in consumer health. For Noom, the new peptide offering extends the company's business beyond weight loss into the broader longevity and wellness market. Hims & Hers signaled months ago that it was ready to tap into the multi-billion-dollar peptide market.

Federal policy shifts and U.S. Food and Drug Administration enforcement discretion around compounded peptides have opened new pathways for telehealth and compounding pharmacies.

On Tuesday, Noom launched OpenRx as a separate peptide and preventive health brand. At launch, OpenRx offers two injectable options: sermorelin, a peptide frequently prescribed for muscle support, and NAD+, a coenzyme frequently prescribed for energy. OpenRx also offers two oral dissolvable tablet options: the first formulation combines the peptides PT-141 and oxytocin with tadalafil to support sexual health. The second ODT formulation is the peptide oxytocin to support intimacy.

Noom says it plans to expand into other areas including recovery, muscle health, skin, gut health and sleep. Peptides are small pieces of protein that occur naturally in the body and help control functions such as growth, healing and appetite.

“Peptides are an important portion of the formulary of healthy aging,” Geoff Cook, CEO of Noom, said in a statement. “OpenRx enables our flagship Noom brand to deepen into cardiometabolic health while the new brand OpenRx supports patients with conditions too often neglected by traditional care models, like energy, muscle composition, skin health, sexual health, sleep, and recovery. Together, both brands support the same mission: to empower everyone, everywhere to live better longer – every day.”

Noom says every OpenRx prescription is written by a licensed clinician following an evaluation of the patient’s health history, goals and clinical appropriateness. Treatments are fulfilled through Noom’s U.S.-based pharmacy network, which operates under state boards of pharmacy oversight and adheres to USP compounding standards, the company said.

Noom is currently reviewing BPC-157 and TB-500 as part of its ongoing process of evaluating emerging treatments for inclusion in our formulary, Jeffrey Egler, M.D., Noom's chief medical officer, said in a statement. "Each therapy offered by OpenRx is selected because our clinical team and I believe it is appropriate for improving patient health. The process involves continuous monitoring of safety-related signals, gathering the judgment of our medical directors and the medical directors of affiliated clinical networks based on years of prescribing experience with the compounds in question, ensuring a compliant and stable supply chain, sourcing of active pharmaceutical ingredients, and setting up processes for compliance with state and federal adverse event reporting guidelines," Egler said.

Online health and wellness brand Hims & Hers announced earlier this month it planned to roll out a peptides business. As part of the company's new Peptides+ specialty, launched today, it plans to initially sell five U.S.-compounded peptide and longevity treatments—Sermorelin, NAD+, Glutathione, Vitamin B12 and L-Carnitine, with plans to add more peptides and therapies over time.

The company also plans to offer U.S.-made BPC-157 and TB-500 "consistent with regulatory requirements," the company said.

A survey the company conducted in October of 2,000 adults found that more than half (55%) said they were interested in or curious about peptide therapies, and 40% of U.S. adults say they are interested or very interested in a telehealth offering of injectable prescription treatments, including peptides and other compounded treatments. Nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults (9%) say they currently use peptides, not including FDA-approved peptides such as Ozempic, Wegovy and insulin, the survey found.

Peptides are in the spotlight due to the massive success of FDA-approved GLP-1 weight loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which are peptide drugs. Wellness influencers and biohackers on social media are promoting other lab-made peptides for fast-tracked healing, anti-aging and muscle growth.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has championed looser federal rules on trendy, unapproved peptide injections. In July, an FDA advisory committee recommended broader access to six unapproved peptides. The panel recommended adding these six substances to the Section 503A Bulks List, which would remove the restrictions on how they are produced by compounders, Fierce Pharma reported.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Kennedy has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued in late October, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

But medical experts have raised safety and clinical evidence questions around unapproved or experimental compounds. The American Medical Association (AMA) publicly opposes the Trump administration’s plan to make certain unapproved peptides more widely available for human use.

In a letter (PDF) to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the AMA pushed back what it called a "rushed" decision to permit the compounding of certain peptides because they have not been approved for safe use by the FDA.

Unproven peptides may pose serious health risks, including allergic reactions, infections, hormonal imbalances and other unexpected side effects, according to the FDA website.

"We should not bypass the science and put patients at risk by making them guinea pigs for unapproved drugs," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement. "If these substances are safe and effective, the evidence should demonstrate that through the FDA’s rigorous review process."

Hims & Hers' peptide therapy program provides a "clinically guided, personalized plan" for consumers "backed by a licensed provider who understands these therapies," according to Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., chief medical officer of the Hims brand.

Hims & Hers wants to "set the standard" for peptide therapy and offer consistency in the quality of the products, Vinjamoori said in an interview on the sidelines of the HLTH conference this week.

"If you think about what we have to bring to the table with our scale and resources, I would argue there's no one better equipped to do it than us," Vinjamoori said.

Hims & Hers has invested in its supply chain and expanded its domestic manufacturing facilities. In 2025, the company acquired a Menlo Park peptide facility to run API validation and stability testing to support its specialized peptide offerings.

"That's why we're investing in our supply chain and doing a lot of the hard work that, frankly, is not the fastest path to making these available. There are pharmacies that are already out there that are making these available, and there are companies out there that will simply just plug into those pharmacies and service patients. But there are inconsistencies," he noted.

Until now, getting these types of medications has often meant relying on unreliable and unregulated online sellers, or a high-cost longevity clinic, Hims & Hers executives said. Hims & Hers' peptides offering gives consumers more accessible care, "backed by real medical leadership and with consistent clinical oversight," the company said in a press release.

Hims & Hers believes its scale gives it an opportunity and responsibility to help build the evidence base around peptides, using growing patient interest not just to expand access but to better understand how the treatments can be used safely and effectively, Vinjamoori said.

Expanding into peptides fits with Hims & Hers' ongoing focus on personalized health, he noted. "We started with sexual health, moved on to hair loss, and then we've continued to broaden into other categories such as hormone replacement, GLP-1s, and now peptides, and many others to come. And the common theme in all of this is that we're talking about helping people accomplish a specific goal that they have. We're not talking about curing a disease or treating a disease per se," he said. "We're talking about, 'Hey, there's something you want to do in your life that you're not able to do right now. Let's help you figure out how we can put together a plan to help you accomplish that."

"This is a big part of the future of medicine itself," Vinjamoori added. "It's been the missing part of the equation, where we've been very focused on treating and responding to disease, but not as much, not just on prevention, but really on helping people use their health as an asset and as a tool to help them accomplish what they want in life."

With Hims & Hers' peptide therapy offering, consumers start with a clinical visit with a licensed provider that includes a comprehensive intake of health history and goals. The company said a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies assesses each individual and, if appropriate, tailors a personalized protocol to their needs.

Hims & Hers treatments are compounded in the U.S. and dispensed directly by licensed, U.S. pharmacies regulated by state boards of pharmacy and "held to rigorous quality and safety standards," the company said.

The buzz around peptides ties into consumers' growing interest in taking control of their health "driven by the cultural zeitgeist moment," Vinjamoori told Fierce Healthcare.

"There's a variety of different factors that catalyze that. I think the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a lot of it for a variety of reasons. I think you see accelerations in biotechnology where people now see something like GLP-1s that can help with a problem that seemed intractable before. I think people are now interested in figuring out what is the range of solutions that could help me. I also think peptides represent something that has a lot of promise, a lot of excitement," he said.

"But there are also some cautions that we need to take as well. Something we think a lot about is how do we meet this moment of excitement and enthusiasm with some degree of rigor and guardrails," Vinjamoori said.

"It starts with the product itself. How do we ensure the quality? The compounds are of the highest quality and are compounded in the most rigorous way, made available in the most rigorous way. That's why we are trying to have as much oversight as we can into the full process of making these available," he said.

He asserted that informed consent and transparency with consumers are critical. "I've spent a lot of time with the team to make sure that we understand that people have this enthusiasm, but we need to make sure that they understand what they're getting into. There is a difference between this and FDA-approved therapies," he said.

"Sometimes people should try the standard of care before they engage with some of these things, and so we want to make sure we have these conversations with people openly and honestly. But at the same time, we also want to respect their choice," he added.

Hims & Hers Peptides+ is available with its Care+ program that gives customers access to twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress, unlimited support and ongoing check-ins from a dedicated care team. Customers can also message providers trained in peptide therapy 24/7 with any questions. The Hims Men’s panel includes at-home blood collection and access to lab tests that provide insights across 22 biomarkers, including testosterone, vitamin D, and cholesterol. The Hers Women’s panel tests 22 biomarkers across hormones, vitamins, and heart health.

#5586. Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

For years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

"I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world."

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an important distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness

To explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

"We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles said. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile."

The online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others showed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

During the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

To introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

After completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results showed that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

When participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

The pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

Further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

"If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he said. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse."

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

The issue has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

The problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

After spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we currently are," he said, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have."

Materials provided by University of Florida. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5585. HLTH 2026: Viz.ai executive shares lessons from effort to expand AI adoption at rural hospitals

HLTH 2026: Viz.ai executive shares lessons from effort to expand AI adoption at rural hospitals" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It’s been almost seven months since artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform Viz.ai entered into a partnership with the National Rural Health Association (NRHA).

The partnership aims to help rural healthcare leaders better understand and implement AI tools across systems. That's been a personal and professional passion of Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim, M.D., who discussed with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH his key takeaways from the collaboration thus far and forward-looking goals as it approaches its one-year mark.

Ibrahim said that the two organizations have done three educational events for rural health systems since the partnership kicked off in April. These series aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI—and whether they should adopt it, he said.

He noted there’s “sometimes a very big mismatch” when smaller rural health systems onboard multiple vendors.

“We've learned [that] many rural hospitals don't have the IT expertise and infrastructure to adopt some of these tools, and so it's actually been a force function to strengthen their hub spoke relationships,” Ibrahim said.

Strengthening these relationships, according to Ibrahim, has been key.

“It's actually been beautiful to see the hub-spoke relationship strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit,” Ibrahim said. “And it gives them a reason to interact more, and a way for the rural hospitals to strengthen their capabilities.”

He continued, “there's an authenticity about the moment where it's like ‘Yeah, we do need to help each other out.’ We're all kind of figuring it out as we go.”

In addition to the educational series, Ibrahim said frameworks are in development to aid rural health systems in navigating, implementing and deploying AI—which will be built into a toolkit.

One of Ibrahim’s personal goals for the one-year mark of the partnership is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when pitched.

“I think that would be a huge milestone,” he said. “Getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal—probably unrealistic, but that's probably the ultimate goal.”

And when it comes to metrics for measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim said he's looking for numbers that show participants are “keeping more care local” and retaining their workforces.

“It would be great to be able to connect the dots [and understand whether] adoption of an AI tool give[s] rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm, willingness to stay in their community as opposed to dropping the services and moving back,” he said.

Another initiative from Viz that has “disproportionate benefit in rural communities,” according to Ibrahim, is its new partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

“I'm pretty excited about being able to bring their level of clinical decision support into our rural hospitals,” he said.

#5584. New Option Approved for Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors

— Adding bezuclastinib to sunitinib improved median PFS by 7 months

The FDA approved the selective KIT inhibitor bezuclastinib (Ekitna), in combination with sunitinib (Sutent), for previously treated gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST).

The approval allows use of the combination in adults with advanced GIST previously treated with imatinib.

"With today's FDA approval of bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib, we have a new standard-of-care treatment following imatinib for patients with GIST," said Andrew Wagner, MD, PhD, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, in an announcement from bezuclastinib-developer Cogent Biosciences. "This approval represents a major step forward for the GIST community and reflects the tireless progress made in improving the lives of people living with this disease."

Sara Rothschild, executive director of the GIST advocacy organization The Life Raft Group, called the approval "an incredibly meaningful milestone for the GIST community that has waited many years hoping, advocating, and helping advance the research for a new treatment option."

Principal support for the approval came from the randomized, international PEAK trial involving 413 patients with locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic GIST and disease progression after or intolerance to imatinib. Patients were randomized to sunitinib alone or in combination with bezuclastinib, and the primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) by independent review. Crossover to the combination was allowed after confirmed progression with single-agent sunitinib.

The primary analysis showed a median PFS of 16.5 months with the combination versus 9.2 months with sunitinib monotherapy. The difference translated into a 50% reduction in the PFS hazard (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.39-0.65, P<0.0001). Significantly more patients randomized to the combination achieved objective responses (46% vs 26%, P<0.0001). Overall survival data remained immature.

Adverse reactions to the combination occurring in ≥20% of patients consisted of diarrhea, increased liver enzymes, hypertension, dysgeusia, hair color changes, fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, decreased appetite, stomatitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, rash, dyspepsia, and pyrexia. The most common (≥5%) grade 3/4 laboratory abnormalities were increased alanine aminotransferase and decreased leukocytes, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and hemoglobin.

The approval brings to six the number of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) for GIST. Imatinib remains the only TKI approved for first-line treatment. Sunitinib alone and the bezuclastinib-sunitinib combination are the only approved second-line therapies. Regorafenib (Stivarga) is approved for use in third line and ripretinib (Qinlock) for fourth line and beyond. Additionally, avapritinib (Ayvakit) has approval for unresectable/metastatic GIST harboring a PDGFRA exon 18 mutation.

Bezuclastinib also is being investigated as a potential treatment for systemic mastocytosis.

#5583. Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis

A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but new research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference. A clinical trial led by researchers at La Trobe University found that supervised exercise and education can improve knee health, reduce pain, and enhance quality of life in young adults recovering from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The findings also offer hope for addressing their elevated risk of developing knee osteoarthritis at an unusually young age.

Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected. About half of patients are still dissatisfied with their knee health two years after the procedure. Even more concerning, roughly half develop signs of early-onset knee osteoarthritis within a decade, often before reaching age 40.

Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations. One obstacle is the widespread concern, shared by some patients and healthcare professionals, that exercise could damage already vulnerable knee cartilage.

A New Approach to Recovery After ACL Surgery

To investigate whether additional rehabilitation could help, researchers at La Trobe University's Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre conducted the SUPER-Knee clinical trial. It was the first study to evaluate the benefits of combining exercise therapy and education more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a time when patients are generally expected to have recovered even though many continue to experience problems.

The researchers enrolled 184 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 who were still struggling with knee symptoms one to three years after their operations. Participants were assigned to either a progressive exercise therapy program or a comparison group that received a single educational session.

The findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, showed that participants who completed the four-month program under the guidance of a physical therapist experienced improvements in knee health and muscle strength, along with less pain and better quality of life.

Importantly, these benefits came without evidence that the exercises were damaging knee cartilage or worsening early osteoarthritis. The results challenge the belief that physical activity necessarily makes injured knees worse.

Exercise Offers Hope Against Early Knee Osteoarthritis

Associate Professor Adam Culvenor, who led the research, said the findings provide much-needed evidence about how to help younger patients who remain at risk of knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery.

"Currently we don't have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority," Associate Professor Culvenor said.

"Our study showed physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.

"The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to update international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.

"The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training."

The findings could influence how clinicians approach rehabilitation long after ACL surgery, particularly for patients whose symptoms continue beyond the usual recovery period. Although the trial did not establish whether the program prevents osteoarthritis over the long term, it demonstrated that supervised exercise can improve knee health without accelerating the cartilage damage or early osteoarthritis researchers were monitoring.

Years of Knee Pain After a Serious Sports Injury

For Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovering from ACL surgery were deeply personal. In 2019, when she was 24, she tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football. Hoping to return to the sport as quickly as possible, she underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks.

But the operation did not lead to the recovery she had imagined. Her rehabilitation continued for years, and she ultimately decided not to return to football.

"I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I'd be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life - not just footy - I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven't played contact sport since," Ruby said.

"Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me."

Cumming remained committed to her rehabilitation, regularly attending physical therapy appointments and performing prescribed exercises. She initially exercised daily before moving to a weekly routine. Despite those efforts, she continued to experience varying degrees of knee pain every day for three to four years.

Her experience changed after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee trial and began participating in weekly rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physical therapist.

"When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly," Ruby said.

The research suggests that people who continue to struggle after ACL reconstruction may benefit from additional structured rehabilitation, even years after their original injury. Because the program requires little specialized equipment or additional staff training, researchers say healthcare professionals could readily incorporate it into existing treatment services.

The SUPER-Knee clinical trial received funding through a Project Grant from Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

#5582. Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists

Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The U.S. Department of Labor proposed new policy this week that would end fast-track green cards for healthcare professionals like nurses and physical therapists—the latest in a string of policies from the Trump administration raising the bar for foreign-born workers and students across healthcare and other industries.

Currently, nurses, physical therapists and other workers “with exceptional ability in the sciences or arts” are granted an exemption from an administrative test in the permanent labor certification program (PERM), a months-long administrative process in which an employer must prove there are no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers for a permanent job ahead of sponsoring a foreign worker.

The exemption, referred to Schedule A, is given to occupations where the DOL recognizes a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers. Nurses and physical therapists have been listed under Schedule A for more than 30 years.

The Department of Labor, in its newly proposed rule, said it wants to eliminate Schedule A as it cannot “demonstrate that the occupations currently listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations.”

It cited in the proposed rule a late 2023 request for information published under the Biden administration seeking input on potentially expanding Schedule A. Despite more than 2,000 responses, DOL now says it didn’t receive the information it would need to establish a methodology for regularly reviewing and updating Schedule A occupations, and questioned whether it has the statutory authority to make such occupational exemptions in the first place.

“The elimination of Schedule A would enable the Department to better ensure that U.S. workers have an opportunity to apply for available job opportunities, and adhere to the statutory requirements to protect U.S. workers assigned to it, as intended by Congress under the [Immigration and Nationality Act].”

The proposed rule, which is open to public comment for 60 days, also includes requirements for employers to advertise their open jobs more broadly and for a longer period of time to demonstrate a good-faith effort to recruit American workers before turning to a green card sponsorship. These and other proposed changes would be the first “comprehensive” reforms to the PERM program in almost two decades, the Department of Labor said.

If finalized as-is, employers who want to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and other affected roles “would be required to go through the lengthier and costlier PERM labor market testing process, adding time, cost and administrative work to a pathway that hospitals, nursing homes and rehabilitation providers have historically relied on to fill persistent shortages,” Caroline Tang, an Austin shareholder at labor and employment law firm Ogletree Deakins, told Fierce Healthcare.

Industry associations as well as other sections of the government have widely projected shortages in the healthcare workforce, including nurses, for the coming years. The Heart Resources and Services Association’s National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, for instance, projects (PDF) national shortages of registered nurses through at least 2038, with a projected 8% shortage in 2028 that is more severe in non-metro areas.

The proposed policy change is among several brought by the Trump administration in line with an order from the White House to prioritize domestic hiring—though many have been stymied in the courts.

Among the most prominent is a $100,000 supplemental fee the Department of Homeland Security attached to H-1B petitions that was vacated by two separate judged, and in August was succeeded by the somewhat altered proposal of an additional H-1B petition fee of $103,265. Another policy from the same department tightening how long nonimmigrant students may remain in the country (referred to as “duration of status”) was temporary blocked hours before implementation in September and fully vacated on Monday (PDF), though the former decision is already being appealed.

The Department of Labor has also proposed increasing the prevailing wage floors for several green cards that legal experts expect will be challenged by employers that would shoulder the resulting financial burden.

#5581. Innovaccer expands Gravity Voice AI agents with SpaceXSI’s Grok Voice model

Healthcare artificial intelligence company Innovaccer Inc. today announced that it has expanded its Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice, the speech-to-speech model from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company SpaceXSI, formerly xAI.

The integration is aimed at the routine calls that make up much of a health system’s phone traffic, such as booking a visit, refilling a prescription or asking about a bill.

Grok Voice is a speech-to-speech model from SpaceXSI that is said to offer subsecond time to first audio, native tool use and the ability to reason while it speaks. According to Innovaccer, the model was trained on real phone audio with interruptions, corrections and background noise in it. More than 25 languages are supported. A business associate agreement is available for Grok Voice, which is Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act-eligible.

Coming into the expansion, Innovaccer’s voice business has grown quickly. Patient voice interactions on the platform have gone from roughly 250,000 to more than five million in the six months since the agents went live. Customers using them are said to be booking significantly more appointments, with referral intakes tripled and documentation time per case down 90%.

“Healthcare Voice AI is moving from answering questions to doing work,” co-founder and Chief Executive Abhinav Shashank said. With Grok Voice, he said, the company is extending where its agents work across the healthcare journey.

Innovaccer’s Agents of Care on Gravity approach is designed so that software handles the bulk of administrative calls, such as scheduling and refills. A human stays in the loop on clinical conversations.

Existing customers will get Grok Voice first through upgrades, along with new customer deployments. Innovaccer plans to use it in scheduling, referrals, prior authorizations, refill requests, chronic care check-ins and annual wellness visit outreach, among other tasks.

The integration is set to extend beyond voice over time. Innovaccer says it will bring Grok models to its healthcare data through the Grok API, with plans for SpaceXSI’s Grok Build coding agent and Grok Bot AI agent as well. Healthcare-specific training and evaluation are to follow once the voice integration is live.

The integration comes about six weeks after SpaceXSI released Grok Voice 3.0, the latest version of the model. At the time, SpaceXSI said Starlink uses Grok Voice to answer about 20,000 customer calls a day, with roughly 70% resolved without a human. The SpaceXSI name was adopted earlier in October, following SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI in February and a rename to SpaceXAI in July.

Innovaccer is a venture capital-backed company that has raised about $675 million to date, including a $275 million Series F round in January 2025. Notable customers include Orlando Health, Adventist HealthCare and Banner Health.

Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice capabilities are available now.

#5580. The Power of Schema Markup: A Comprehensive Guide for Real Estate Agents

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

Implementing Schema Markup for Real Estate

UnitedHealthcare is teaming up with CPSEN for a new program that will lean on community pharmacists to reach Medicaid patients.

The insurance giant said Wednesday that its through the UHC Pharmacy Care Hub model, pharmacists will work alongside the payer's care managers and providers to help close gaps in care and support management for chronic conditions and other needs.

Participating pharmacies will offer a range of services, including telehealth, medication management, point-of-care testing and personalized supports. The program is built on a hub-and-spoke model, where pharmacists can then help lead the patient to the right site of care or through any follow-up if needed.

These interactions can also help track patterns in emergency care use, and help patients find a more appropriate setting if their needs aren't emergent.

The program is currently available to UnitedHealthcare Medicaid members in seven states: Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. UHC expects to add additional states throughout the year.

Part of the goal, the company said, is to tap into the trust that local pharmacists have in the communities they serve.

“Community pharmacies are trusted, local access points for care,” said Arethusa Kirk, M.D., chief medical officer for UnitedHealthcare Community & State, in the announcement. “This new model expands the services independent pharmacists can help deliver, making it easier for people—especially those facing barriers to care—to get timely support closer to home.”

UHC said that most (89%) of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy, making these locations an easier option to access for many. This is especially true for individuals who may struggle to find an appointment with a doctor or find transportation to a visit.

For example, a participating pharmacist in North Carolina, Madeline Clark, said in the announcement that a patient came into the pharmacy for a urine test, as she had a potential urinary tract infection. The pharmacy conducted the test and sent the results virtually to a provider through UnitedHealthcare's Doctor Chat tool.

A prescription was then filled for the patient in the same visit, and she was out the door within about 30 minutes.

Clark said the patient was thankful not just for the ease of that trip to the pharmacy but for avoiding a visit to the ER as well.

"Not only was this a lower cost of care in the healthcare system space, but it also was just incredibly helpful for the patient," she said.

#5578. A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math

For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies

To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important.

The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children

An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes."

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

#5577. AI Helped Hospital Lower Readmissions, Deaths After Discharge

— EMR-based tool alerted clinicians to highest-risk patients in need of closer follow-up

Artificial intelligence (AI) helped one Texas hospital lower readmissions and post-discharge deaths, without adding any new staff, according to a case study presented at the HLTH conference in Las Vegas.

Using predictive AI to focus follow-up visits on its Medicare surgical patients at highest risk, Houston Methodist Hospital's 30-day post-discharge mortality fell about 35%, and readmissions fell about 18%, Brenda Campbell, MS, BSN, the hospital's senior innovation consultant, said at the conference.

Observed-to-expected (O/E) ratios -- which compare patients' results with those of Medicare patients matched for baseline risk -- fell from 0.48 in 2021-2022 to 0.31 in 2025-Q1 2026 (a partial period) for post-discharge deaths. Meanwhile, the O/E ratio for readmissions fell from 1.17 to 0.96 over the same period. A falling O/E ratio means the hospital moved faster than the benchmark, she reported.

Clinician follow-up visits within 14 days rose from 54.6% to 62.2% in the highest mortality-risk group and from 55.8% to 64.5% in the highest readmission-risk group during that time. Crucially, the hospital said this was accomplished without adding staff.

"We've done this without any additional resources," Campbell said. "Resources are tight. ... You have to really risk-stratify to get the right patients to the resources that you have."

The effort began in 2021, when Houston Methodist Hospital asked why its cardiovascular service line ranked well for inpatient mortality but poorly after discharge. The hospital brought in the Health Data Analytics Institute (HDAI), which had trained predictive AI on the entire Medicare data set, including 150 million Medicare lives.

HDAI found the cardiovascular service line ranked 7th for in-hospital mortality but 43rd for 30-day post-discharge mortality among more than 100 academic medical centers. About 70% of the 30-day post-discharge deaths occurred in the highest-risk quintile of patients.

"You can't manage what you don't know," Campbell said.

The hospital created a risk stratification plan, with predictions embedded into the electronic medical record. It asked clinicians to prioritize follow-up within 2 weeks for the highest-risk patients.

"Your limited team can't see everybody. ... So let's get to the people who are most likely to readmit," Carola Endicott, EdM, vice president of customer engagement at HDAI, said at the conference.

Timely follow-up can be life-saving, Endicott said in an interview after the session. A patient might be experiencing shortness of breath they don't feel is urgent enough to call about, she said. They may have forgotten to pick up a potentially crucial prescription medication, and need a friendly reminder. Or perhaps there was a surgical complication that wasn't caught.

John Brownstein, PhD, senior vice president and chief innovation officer at Boston Children's Hospital, who was not involved in the initiative, called it a "really concrete application of AI to predict high-risk groups that are worthy of intervention in a way that reduces the risk of readmission and mortality."

"AI can level the playing field," Brownstein told MedPage Today. "Well-funded health systems can hire staff to compensate for some of these challenges, but in a world where you are understaffed, AI can help reach those goals."

By working with clinicians to prioritize efforts, Houston Methodist Hospital's readmission ranking among 114 academic medical centers, among all medical and surgical Medicare fee-for-service patients, rose from 59th in 2022 to 7th in 2024, based on actual-to-expected rates, Campbell reported.

Mortality and readmission post-discharge is a major metric that hospitals track, said Brownstein. "It's a big cost to health systems and it is a big impact for patients. That's why so many health systems have invested in this space."

For Brownstein, this case study shows that implementing AI solutions doesn't have to be overcomplicated. "We want the right tool for the right problem. We over-index on these high-token use cases for generative AI. In this case, this use case is straightforward, and really high-value."

"We think it's the small things really that can have the biggest impact," Campbell said. She would like to see the follow-up rate climb further. "We're not where we want to be, but we know we're on the right trajectory to get there."

Aetna is rolling out a new program that aims to provide key end-to-end care for pregnant women, new mothers and infants.

The offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna plan. Through the program, moms will be connected to a prenatal visit in their first trimester and a postpartum visit within 12 weeks of the baby's birth.

Women in the program will also be screened for depression both during and after pregnancy to identify any risks.

In addition to supporting the mother both during pregnancy and postpartum, the program aims to give babies a healthy start by providing at least six well visits through their first 15 months, which offer critical tests and screenings, checkups and vaccinations.

The news of the launch was provided first to Fierce Healthcare.

Katerina Guerraz, Aetna's chief operating officer, told Fierce that maternal care often focuses mostly, if not completely, on labor and delivery, though prenatal and postpartum visits play a critical role in driving positive health outcomes.

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access issue, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she said.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz said.

Aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she said.

Aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the company to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz said that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she said.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz said the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she said.
